items.text: **Clean up test rows my audit wrote to the live database** **Why:** during the 2026-10-06 playtest audit my random-click testing submitted some in-game feedback ("yes"/"no") rows and a few anonymous saves to production before I added a write-blocker. The API has no delete route, so only you can remove them (Neon SQL editor). Details and the exact SQL, with a preview query to run first, are at the bottom of `planning/AUDIT-261006.md`. **Steps:** run the two `SELECT` previews, check the rows are test data (the date filter may also match real submissions from 5 Oct), then run the `DELETE`s. Tell me once done and I will remove this entry.

**PC version of every game: send screenshots when all are done** **Your answer (2026-10-07): later.** When every game has its Desktop layout (all 14 now have one, committed 2026-10-07; I have not taken the screenshots yet, they cost usage and I am saving it for the weekly reset), I send screenshots of all of them and you give your input. Nothing needed from you until then. Controller support: not yet; audio stays parked.

**Apply for Google AdSense** **Your answer (2026-10-07): later.** Kept here so it is not forgotten. **Why:** `planning/pwa-and-ads-setup.md`'s ad bar is already built and labeled everywhere on the site, wired up with placeholder IDs (`ca-pub-XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX`) waiting for the real ones. The only blocker is the application itself, which needs your own Google account — I can't submit it for you. **Steps:** 1. Confirm the hub is live over HTTPS at its real public GitHub Pages URL (it already should be — this is just a sanity check before applying). 2. Go to Google AdSense (google.com/adsense) and apply using that URL and your own Google account. 3. Approval can take anywhere from days to weeks — applying doesn't commit you to anything, so it's worth doing early even if you're not in a rush. 4. If AdSense asks you to add a verification snippet or an `ads.txt` file before/during review, hold off — send me the exact text they give you (see below) and I'll add it correctly rather than you hand-editing site files. **What to tell me once you have it:** - The `ca-pub-XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX` client ID AdSense gives you. - Your ad unit's slot ID. - The exact `ads.txt` line, if AdSense gave you one. I'll drop all of that into the ad bar and it goes live everywhere on the site at once, since it's a shared partial.

**Chronicle: spot-check the weakest claims first: "Washington added 'so help me God'" (two of its three sources are opinion essays from one outlet)?** Open `games/chronicle/review.html` on the dev server and tell me keep, fix or drop.

**Chronicle: spot-check the Sputnik to Apollo 11 cause link (no single source states the whole chain)?** Open `games/chronicle/review.html`; recommend keeping it labelled "contributing" unless you want it dropped.
**Chronicle: spot-check the Lincoln-stayed-at-the-Wills-house claim (only NPS pages and one exhibition place him there)?** Tell me keep, fix or drop.
**Chronicle: spot-check the Fort Sumter options claim (only two institutions) and the 1792 second-term decision (one Miller Center line plus one NCC line)?** Tell me keep, fix or drop for each.
**Chronicle: are the 14 passage summaries in "Whose account?" fair and balanced in tone?** I wrote them from fetched page summaries, not whole pages, so a skim by you is the check.

**Lighthouse: it shipped with 21 achievements (11 for keeping the light, 10 story ones, six of them hidden until solved) instead of the plan's 16; should I cut it to 16?** Recommended: keep 21, since you like reachable 100% and every one is earnable in a Quiet year.

**Lighthouse: a night lasts about 3 minutes at normal speed (one tick per 4 seconds); is that the right pace, or should it be faster or slower?** Recommended: keep 3 minutes, with 2x and 4x speeds and pause already available.

**FREN152: the slides folder holds "FREN152 LECTURE 13 (2024)", a 2024 lecture 13 although week 13 has not happened this semester; should I use it as a preview of week 13 or ignore it?** Recommended: ignore it until your 2026 week 13 arrives, since the 2024 content may differ from this year's.

**Logic Gates: it ships with a small story (a station called Meridian Relay and a flawed previous engineer called Vale who left notes); keep it, or make the game pure puzzle?** Recommended: keep it (it is switchable in settings, and the engineer is not an all-good hero). Say "yes" to keep it.

**Logic Gates: should a level open as soon as the chips it needs are unlocked (so the order is partly free), or strictly one after another?** Recommended: chip-based (the current build), since you like objectives without a strict order. Say "yes" to keep it.
**Logic Gates: keep "par" (fewest chips) as an optional second mark on each level?** Recommended: yes, kept generous and optional, never needed to progress.

**Robot Script: should the free sandbox open earlier than the end of the last chapter (for example after chapter 3)?** Recommended: open it after chapter 3 so there is somewhere to experiment sooner. Say "yes" to go with that.

**Robot Script: is the companion drone Scrap's tone right (quiet, dry, slightly sulky salvage drone, not a cheerful hero)?** Recommended: yes, keep it quiet and a little sulky. Say "yes" to go with that.
**Robot Script: is the medal rule right (gold for the reference length, silver for up to a third more, bronze for any clear)?** Recommended: yes, as written. Say "yes" to go with that.

**Robot Script: should chapter 1 stay straight corridors with no turning, or bring turning in from room 4?** Recommended: bring turning in from room 4 so chapter 1 teaches more. Say "yes" to go with that.

**Robot Script: chapters currently open after 5 of 7 rooms are cleared; do you prefer every room open from the start?** Recommended: open every room from the start, since you like objectives without a strict order. Say "yes" to go with that.

**Dream game: which six keepers (people who run buildings) should be there at launch?** My suggestion, since the first is fixed by your answer: the builder (first, wood quest), a woodcutter, a miner, a librarian, a workshop tinkerer and a healer. Say "yes" to go with that, or name your own.

**Dream game: should I propose three options for the main story (one paragraph each) for you to pick from, or do you want to describe the idea first?** Recommended: I propose three options. Say "yes" for that, or "no" and describe it in a comment.
**App form: if the site gets an installable app, should I look at desktop first or phone first?** Recommended: desktop first (a small desktop wrapper), since you mostly play on PC at night.

**App form: may any game be playable only in the app (flagged "App only" on the hub), or should every game stay on the web?** Recommended: keep every game on the web for now; flag a game "best in the app" later if it needs it (the dream game, maybe).
**App form: shall I try a small desktop-app experiment with one existing game to see how much work it is?** Recommended: yes, later, after the current game batches finish.

**Should Signal's daily puzzle keep a streak, or be a plain "today's puzzle" with no streak?** Recommended: no streak by default, keep the archive so missing a day costs nothing. Reason: you like daily content but daily pressure is what you dislike. Say "yes" to go with that.

**When a puzzle has a hint ladder, should the next rung open only when you press "Another hint"?** Recommended: yes, every rung needs a press and the first rung asks "Would you like a suggestion?". Reason: you want hints only when you agree to them. Say "yes" to go with that.

**In a huge skill tree with no free refund, should a wrong spend be repairable by a paid undo (in-game currency, not a restart)?** Recommended: yes, a small in-game cost to move one point. Reason: it keeps your "no free refund" feeling and your "nothing you cannot get back" rule. Say "yes" to go with that.

**When you want the audio block (clicks, soundtrack, alerts, ambience), should it be before the dream game starts?** Recommended: yes, one block in the next quiet week and a master mute on every game. Reason: you said it happens all at once, and sounds are easier to add before big new games exist. Say "yes" to go with that.

**Can I build three small mockups of overlay windows (a side drawer, a centred pop-up, a full-screen menu) on one test page so you can pick?** Recommended: yes, with a picture for each. Reason: you want overlays on PC but did not know the terms, so seeing them is easier than describing them. Say "yes" to go with that.

**Should Stranded and the other Lifeline-style games have a narrator voice line in text (a short intro per day) rather than silent logs?** Recommended: yes, a short narrated-style intro per day that can be turned off. Reason: you picked a narrator over silence but want story optional. Say "yes" to go with that.

**Should two-player puzzles work with just one friend who has a link, even if the site has very few players?** Recommended: yes, invite link only and a solo version that plays both halves. Reason: only about two friends play today, so it must work with one or none. Say "yes" to go with that.

**Should account-wide titles replace per-game titles?** Recommended: yes, no per-game titles; one titles shelf on your account. Reason: you dislike per-game titles but said account ones could be cool. Say "yes" to go with that.

**Should every game get a "difficulty" choice at the start (easy, normal, hard) even when the game is already easy?** Recommended: yes, with normal as the default and hard shown as an option. Reason: you want multiple difficulties from the start and easy-to-medium as the base. Say "yes" to go with that.

**Hull Repair: is the split right between a board being "patched" (every line joined) and "restored" (every cell covered too), or should patched alone fill the station map?** Recommended: keep both; patched opens the map, restored earns the log line. Say "yes" to go with that.

**Hull Repair: should a deck open once 5 of its 8 boards are patched, or should every board be open from the start?** Recommended: open every board from the start, since you like objectives without a strict order. Say "yes" to go with that.
**Hull Repair: is the quiet station tone right, or should the repair log be shorter or off by default?** Recommended: keep it, with a Settings switch to hide the log. Say "yes" to go with that.
**Hull Repair: should there be a free workbench mode after the last deck (draw your own boards)?** Recommended: yes, later, as a sandbox. Say "yes" to go with that.
**Hull Repair: should valves or mixers arrive earlier than decks 4 and 5?** Recommended: bring valves to deck 3 so they have more boards to prove themselves. Say "yes" to go with that.
**Hull Repair: only two boards reach 9x9 and deck 5 is mostly 8x8; is that fine, or should bigger boards be allowed more colours?** Recommended: fine as is. Say "yes" to go with that.
**Station Medic: should the sheet's "rule out for me" dimming be on by default, with a setting to turn it off?** Recommended: on by default, with the setting. Say "yes" to go with that.

**Station Medic: should a Rough shift (a bad call, then restored with costs) still count toward opening the next chapter?** Recommended: yes, so a bad call never blocks you. Say "yes" to go with that.
**Station Medic: keep "borrow a spare" and "comfort care" (each costs 1) as the no-dead-end fallbacks?** Recommended: keep both. Say "yes" to go with that.
**Station Medic: keep the names Lowlight Station, Tally (the robot) and the absent Dr. Aurel?** Recommended: keep them; say "no" and give new names if you want. Say "yes" to go with that.

**Station Medic: the crew's flaws (hoarded seed stock, an adjusted supply count, a hidden weld report) are gentle but real; should I drop any?** Recommended: keep all of them, since you want characters who are not all good. Say "yes" to go with that.

**Station Medic: chapters open after 5 of 8 shifts are done; do you prefer every chapter open from the start?** Recommended: open every chapter from the start, since you like objectives without a strict order. Say "yes" to go with that.

**Stranded: replies currently appear at once, with a "one message per tap" setting; should one message per tap be the default?** Recommended: yes, one message per tap, since it reads like a conversation and has no timer. Say "yes" to go with that.
**Stranded: Ines is the flawed one and Harbour (you, the voice) is plain; should Harbour have a real flaw too?** Recommended: yes, a small one that shapes a few choices. Say "yes" to go with that.

**Stranded: some replies and endings are locked behind Trust, Supplies or Hope, always with a visible reason and an open alternative; keep that or have no locks at all?** Recommended: keep the visible-reason locks. Say "yes" to go with that.
**Stranded: keep the names Ines Varga, Orrin, Sparrow Relay, Kestrel, Marigold, Bit and Pavel?** Recommended: keep them; say "no" and give new names if you want. Say "yes" to go with that.
**Stranded: the reveal that Pavel flies the relief ship only happens if she opens his message or at the door; keep the twist?** Recommended: keep it. Say "yes" to go with that.

**Stranded: all nine endings are warm or bittersweet and Quiet Line is the saddest; do you want one that is sadder but still gentle?** Recommended: yes, one more, still with no on-screen death. Say "yes" to go with that.

Which game would you like to play in under ten minutes, and what would it need?
Logic Gates: wire AND, OR, NOT and XOR chips to hit target outputs. Each solved level unlocks a new chip, and the last levels have you build a tiny working computer.
Hull Repair: Flow-Free-style routing of power and pipes across a damaged space-station hull. Every solved board repairs one room on a station map, so the puzzles form a bigger picture.
Robot Script: give a robot a short list of instructions to clear a room (Lightbot style). No timer, medals for using fewer steps, and a free sandbox once you finish.
Reaction Bench: balance chemical reactions to synthesise compounds, and fill a periodic table as you discover each element's uses.
Rule Finder: a sequence of numbers or shapes follows a hidden rule; you test guesses and name the rule.
Slingshot: plan fuel burns and gravity assists to reach moons in a simple but real solar-system model, with the planet data read from a named source.
Teach the Machine: train a tiny classifier by choosing which features it looks at, then see exactly why it gets some cases wrong.
Constellations: connect stars by rules to complete real sky maps, collecting each constellation with a short sourced note.
Zero-G Shift: Sokoban-style crate pushing, but everything keeps sliding until it hits something.
Mirror Lab: place mirrors and prisms so a laser reaches every sensor.
Radio Decode: decode binary, hex and simple ciphers from a drifting signal, each message a short log entry.
Picture Grid: nonograms where each solved picture goes into a gallery you can browse.
Station Medic: help the crew of a space station by solving triage puzzles with limited supplies. Nobody dies on screen; a bad call means "restore and try a different plan".
Robot Repair Shop: fix quirky robots by solving their fault puzzles; each repaired robot becomes a friend that gives you a gift later.
Fog Rescue: guide lost animals or travellers out of a dark foggy forest by lighting the right lanterns in the right order.
Water Works: route clean water to villages with trade-offs between town, farm and wild land, shown from several people's points of view.
Derelict Garden: tend a garden on an abandoned ship, restoring one section at a time, with a steady-progress-that-cannot-be-lost feel.
Memory Archivist: restore corrupted memories from a damaged AI by putting scraps back in order (dark, quiet, science fiction).
Food Bank: plan a week of meals and deliveries for a food bank with a limited budget and several families' needs.
Housing Board: allocate a limited set of homes between competing needs and see how each side judges the result.
Anomaly Catalogue: a fixed set of odd rooms or screens where you spot what changed and file it in a field catalogue (the kind of anomaly games you like to watch).
Loadout Lab: combine parts to reach target numbers, with a catalogue of every combination you have found, including the one overpowered build per challenge.
Glitch Hunter: small levels with deliberate, harmless exploits; the goal is to break the rules and the log records every glitch you found.
Space Museum: curate a museum of objects you have collected across the site, arranged in rooms.
Site Codex: one notebook that fills as you play every game (concepts, facts, characters), with a completion percentage.
Trophy Room: a low-poly room on the hub showing a model for each thing you have earned or finished across the site.
A "100% map" page: every game as a node that fills as you complete it, with a clear list of what is left.
A "rarest things you own" strip on the hub, using the existing achievement rarity numbers.
Stranded: you advise a stranded astronaut by text over many branching days; there is no waiting timer, and you can go back and try a different path.
The Quiet Program: advise a broken but gentle program on a failing computer network (a tragic, quiet character in the spirit of the one you like).
Night Cameras: investigate odd events by switching between security cameras; no jump scares, and the answer is a deduction.
Three Sides of the Story: a branching story about a real issue (for example a water shortage), played once from each of three people's viewpoints.
Evidence Hunt: a Phasmophobia-lite deduction game where you collect evidence and name the ghost, solo first with an optional co-op by invite code.
Terminal Logs: a choose-your-own-adventure told only through a computer terminal's logs and your commands.
Keep Talking: two players each see half of a puzzle and have to talk it out (voice or text in whatever app they already use), joined by an invite link.
Shared Station: friends' finished puzzles light up rooms in a shared space station you can visit.
Saboteur Puzzle: a solo logic puzzle where you work out who among the crew is sabotaging the ship from their statements.
Friends-only boards: a private leaderboard group created with an invite code, with a "hide my score" option.
Hint gift: a friend can send you one hint on a puzzle you are stuck on, no text, just a nudge.
Gift an item: send a collected item to a friend once per day, optional and never needed.
Community bar: one shared progress bar that every player's actions fill together toward a goal, cooperative only.

sections.title: Site features that fit how you actually play

items.text: "How long have you got?" button on the hub: pick 5 minutes, 15 minutes or "all night" and it suggests games that fit.
Half-asleep mode: large buttons, dimmed screen, calm games only, one-handed layout.
Warm night colours after 10pm: the hub and games shift to a dimmer, warmer palette automatically (opt-in).
An Ironman switch per game: opt-in hard fail with no restore, with its own badge, never the default.
An "undo my last decision" button in every sim, one level deep.
A graded hint ladder in puzzle games: a nudge, then a hint, then the answer, so you never have to leave to look it up.
Strategy notes page per game: the known good builds and strategies written into the game, so you never alt-tab.
Watch mode for city and sim games: the settlement plays itself slowly so you can leave it on a second screen.
A personal stats page: what you play, when, and how long, so you can see your own pattern.
A "pick up where you stopped" strip on the hub that also shows the exact thing you were doing in each game.
Repair the Ship's Code: learn Python by fixing a starship's broken functions, with tests that go green as you fix each one.
Query the Archive: learn simple database queries by finding records in a space-station archive, no deletion allowed.
Pattern Match: learn regular expressions by filtering garbled transmissions.
Binary Bakery: a calm game where you build numbers from binary switches to fill orders.
Orbit Maths: short maths puzzles in a rocket-launch frame (ratios, speeds, fuel).
Circuit Playground: a free sandbox for building circuits with live voltage readouts.
AI Mistakes: spot where a simple AI would go wrong in a series of small cases and say why.
Material Match: pick materials for a tool or building from their real properties, with the numbers read from a named source.
Joinery: fit differently shaped timber pieces into a frame outline with no gaps; each solved frame unlocks a new building type.
Blueprint balance: place beams so the load on every support stays under its limit; a good result gives sturdier buildings.
Cut list: cut planks from a log to fill a list of orders with the least waste.
Scaffold climb: build a path of plank pieces from the ground to a roof gap within a fixed number of planks.
Tool tidy: sort tools into a rack by size and use so everything fits; a tidy rack makes building faster.
Floor plan puzzle: lay out rooms inside a building outline so every room touches the doors and light it needs.
Log stack: stack uneven logs so the pile does not tip, using a simple balance rule.
Grain reading: match a cut's ring pattern to the right tool and angle.
Sorting belt: route logs by type on a short conveyor with switches.
Replanting map: choose where to replant so the forest edge keeps a clear path to the cabin.
Sharpening: line up a blade's angle by feel (a dial and a visible sparks gauge, no timer).
Forest survey: reveal and mark trees on a fog grid using clues from neighbouring counts (a minesweeper-like deduction).
Vein deduction: numbers on the edges show how much ore lies in each row and column; find the veins (a nonogram-style puzzle).
Shoring: place supports so no tunnel span is too long.
Cart routing: lay track from the face to the lift with turns and switches.
Ventilation: connect fans and shafts so air reaches every working room.
Assay: weigh samples on a balance to find the odd one.
Bunker rooms: open sealed bunker sections by solving each door's lock (logic, symbols or sequences) to unlock a specialisation.
Catalogue sort: shelve books by clues about author, colour and subject.
Torn page: rejoin torn pieces of a page by edges and content.
Cipher margin: decode notes with a key hidden in another book.
Reading order: put a set of letters and journals in the order they must have been written, from the details inside them.
Family tree: fill a tree from scattered records; a completed tree unlocks that family's quest.
Map restoration: place map fragments by matching coastlines and roads.
Circuit bench: build a working circuit from parts to light, move or sense something.
Gear train: connect gears so the output turns at the required speed and direction.
Part salvage: take apart a broken machine into the right parts in the right order.
Calibration: match a gauge reading by adjusting several linked knobs.
Assembly line: arrange stations on a belt to turn parts into a product at the lowest cost (the production line that leads to robots).
Wiring diagram: reconnect a tangled board by following a schematic.
Crop rotation: plan which crop goes in which bed over seasons so the soil recovers.
Watering paths: lay channels to reach every bed with limited pipe.
Seed matching: pair seeds to beds by light, soil and season clues.
Frost cover: place covers on beds so every tender plant is covered with the fewest sheets.
Pollination: guide a few bees through flowers in an order that reaches all of them.
Preserving: pack jars into a shelf so they fit and can be reached.
Recipe mix: combine ingredients to reach a target taste or effect (add and balance sliders).
Label the shelf: deduce which herb is which from smell, colour and use clues.
Boil down: reduce a liquid to an exact amount by choosing heat steps.
Pantry fit: pack a larder so the most-used items sit in reach.
Feast plan: plan courses for guests with likes and dislikes (links to gifting).
Remedy book: discover recipes by combining clues from keepers about what ails them.
Star map: connect stars into a named pattern by rules.
Tuning: find a station by adjusting two dials against a signal-strength meter.
Decode: turn a repeating signal into a message (binary, Morse-like or glyphs).
Aiming: line up a dish with a moving source using stepped turns.
Lens alignment: stack lenses so a beam reaches a sensor.
Sky catalogue: match observations from different nights to find what moved.
Seating plan: seat guests so likes and dislikes are respected.
Story order: arrange a told story's events using clues from several tellers.
Who said it: match statements to speakers from a few hints.
Table game: a small two-player-style logic game against the keeper, solvable without luck.
Song lines: reorder scrambled lines of a verse by rhyme and rhythm marks.
Rumour chain: trace which rumour started where from who told whom.
Heat colours: pick the right heat step for each stage of a piece.
Alloy mix: blend metals to hit target numbers.
Mould fit: choose a mould that fills without gaps from a few pieces.
Forging order: put steps in the right order to avoid cracking (rules shown).
Rivet pattern: place rivets so a plate holds with the fewest.
Repair puzzle: mend a broken tool by fitting back its fragments.
Herb drying: arrange racks so each herb gets the light and air it needs.
Symptom match: deduce what ails a visitor from signs (invented conditions, no real medical advice).
Bandage wrap: a path puzzle where the wrap must cover a shape without overlap.
Candle ritual: light candles in an order that follows a pattern of rules.
Garden of remembrance: place stones and plants by clues about those remembered.
Dream lines: connect matching symbols in a sleeping visitor's dream without crossing.
Term popovers: one shared helper so any game can mark a word, and tapping it shows a one-line plain definition. You get help with jargon in every game without leaving the screen.
Replay the tips: one shared button in each game's settings that brings back the one-time hints you have already dismissed. You get a way back to guidance after a break.
Compare two runs: one shared screen that puts any two finished runs side by side with the differences highlighted. You get the same useful tool in every game that keeps run records.
Run report card: one shared end-of-run screen with your best moment, your worst moment and three choices you might redo. You get the same helpful ending everywhere.
Text view for drawings: a shared helper that describes any drawn scene or map as plain text and tables. You get a way for screen-reader users to follow games that rely on pictures.
Colour-blind palette presets: a shared setting with palettes tuned for the three common kinds of colour blindness. You get readable colour in every game with one choice.
New feature dots: a small dot on any button added since your last visit, which fades once you open it. You get a quiet way to spot what changed.
Try next: a card at the end of a run that suggests one other game on the site that fits what you just enjoyed. You get a natural next step.
Difficulty tier picker: one shared picker with named tiers, a plain summary of what each changes and your best result per tier. You get the same clear choice in every game that has hard modes.
Gamepad support: a shared helper so menus and boards can be moved with a controller. You get a comfortable way to play on a TV or from the sofa.
Plain-words option: a setting that swaps long or technical text for shorter, simpler wording. You get games that are easier to read for everyone.
Extra themes: more colour themes beyond light and dark, such as a warm sepia and a high-contrast amber. You get a choice that suits your eyes and your room.
Loading tips: while a game loads, show a short tip and the last thing you did there. You get something useful to read during the wait.
Run notes: a one-line note you can attach to any save or finished run, such as what you were trying. You get a way to remember your own ideas.
Photo mode: one shared button that hides all menus for a clean screenshot. You get nice pictures of your work from any game.
Help search: pressing the help key opens a search box over every help panel in the current game. You get an answer in seconds without scrolling.
Consistent menu corner: the menu, settings and help buttons sit in the same place in every game. You get less hunting when you switch between games.
Three goals everywhere: roll the three-goals panel out beyond the first four games to every game, each fed by its own goals. You get the layout you like in every game.
Session goal: when you open a game, pick "quick" or "all night" and set your own goal, and the game closes the session with a note that you hit it. You get the pride of a self-set goal.
Note for tomorrow: before you leave a game you can write yourself one sentence, which greets you on your next visit. You get a friendly welcome back that you wrote.
Finds: the games notice unusual strategies, such as closing Loop without trade, and list them as finds with a short name. You get credit for clever builds.
Played together: if two friends play the same game on the same day, both get a small cosmetic badge. You get an optional friend tie with no chat and no ranking.
Robot companion: a tiny customisable robot that appears on welcome-back screens and gains parts from achievements across games. You get a character designer feel and a reason to collect.
Long-night route: the hub suggests a three-stop route across games for a long session, one calm, one thinking and one building, with no timers. You get a plan for a three-hour night.
How I play presets: one choice of calm, collector or speed that flips hints, effects and display settings in every game. You get the site set up for you in one tap.
Account ranks: titles that rise with your total across all games, shown on your profile and cards. You get account-wide titles (your account-title taste).
Lifetime site counter: a big counter of everything you have done across the site, such as units moved or plots watered. You get growth that feels huge (your big-number taste).
Session overlay: a small corner panel in any game showing this session's progress, like a mission view. You get a mission-style progress view (your taste for a goals panel).
Add-a-note button: a note button in every game that fills in the game and area and sends your note to the ideas sheet. You get a fast way to log playtest thoughts (your play-test list habit).
Friend kind notes: short preset notes from friends appear on your welcome-back screen. You get a friend tie with no chat (your gifts-and-notes taste).
Co-op rooms: any game can open a two-person invite link and swap one tiny message per turn. You get a base for co-op puzzles (your Keep Talking taste).
App edition: package the site as a desktop and phone app with a few extras that work offline. You get an app-style site (your app-form dream).
Completion perks: your completion percent in each game unlocks a small account-wide cosmetic. You get a reason to finish games (your reachable-100% taste).
Low-energy shelf: a hub row of games you can play half asleep. You get a quick pick for tired nights (your half-asleep taste).
Time-of-day greeting: the hub greets you differently late at night, kindly and without guilt. You get a friendly welcome back (your welcome-back taste).
Suggest on request: a site-wide "Would you like a suggestion?" that only responds when you ask. You get help only when you want it (your suggestion-only-if-asked taste).
Comfort card: on your first visit, four ticks for text size, motion, contrast and simple words apply to every game. You get a site that works for anyone (your accessible-to-everyone taste).
Party table: a host screen with phones as controllers for short friend-night games. You get a Jackbox-style night with friends (your friends-play-Jackbox taste).
Impostor in the lab: a small-group deduction game where one player has a different rule, and you talk it out in any app. You get an Among Us-style night (your Among Us taste).
Site factions: join a faction such as Gridkeepers or Tidewatch and earn standing from related games for cosmetic rewards. You get many ways to play (your taste for factions and many ways to play).
Host AI: an optional hub voice with dry, dark remarks about your total progress, never about mental health. You get a GLaDOS-style host (your Portal taste).
Stuck helper: after a while with no progress, a gentle choice offers a nudge, an easier setting or parking it with a note. You get help before you quit (your quit-if-stuck habit).
Good stopping points: natural end-of-session markers with no timers. You get an easy place to stop (your perfectionism-burnout concern).
People helped counter: a site-wide count of every relief, rescue and care action across games. You get proof of your helper role (your healer taste).
Doodle booth: a simple pad to draw your own stickers and icons for your profile. You get a hand-drawn touch (your willing-to-make-rough-art taste).
Process timeline: a page that turns the dev logs and change lists into a tidy timeline for your coursework. You get evidence ready for class (your devlog-formality request).
Fully reachable badge: each game shows a verified checklist of what 100 percent means. You get no hidden requirements (your reachable-100% taste).

Add a "why is this slow?" button on any resource or building that names the one thing holding it back (for example "Sky Cities on Venus are waiting on 28 more Mars Regolith") and jumps you to the fix. You stop guessing and always know the next useful step.

Add an orbital depot: a shared warehouse where any world can park surplus and any other world can draw from it, upgradeable in size. You get a simple way to smooth out shortages without setting up a route for every pair of worlds.

Give every world one signature building with its own special rule (for example a Venus scrubber that makes neighbouring worlds' ecology decay slower). Each world then plays a little differently and you have a reason to revisit finished worlds.

Add fork nodes to the research tree: at a few points you pick one of two upgrades, and you can swap later for a small fee so no choice is permanent. You get meaningful build choices without any risk of getting stuck.

Add an "auto-pause on important moments" setting that pauses the game when a research finishes, a world completes, or ecology drops under 15%. You can leave the game running and never miss the moment that matters.
Add a trade map in the Overview showing which worlds ship what to which, with thicker lines for bigger flows. You see the whole economy at a glance instead of opening each route.

Add a soft early warning when ecology is heading toward the penalty zone at the current rate ("Ecology reaches 10% in about 40 ticks") with the cheapest fix suggested. You can prevent trouble instead of reacting to it.
Show "affordable in about N seconds" next to every Buy button, based on current income. You can plan purchases instead of watching numbers.
Add a hover preview on each world in the Overview showing what finishing its terraforming will unlock. You can choose which world to focus on for a reason.
Let finished worlds collapse to a single quiet line in the Overview, with a tap to expand. The screen stays tidy in the late game and you still reach any world in one tap.

Add alternate openings: begin the system on Mars or Venus instead of Earth, each with a fixed starting kit and its own early order of unlocks. You get a new way to replay the whole game that is planned, not random.

Add a "status in three sentences" button that describes the whole system in plain words (which worlds are running, what is short, what is next). Screen reader users and tired players get the full picture without scanning every card.

Add handcrafted rescue worlds: short puzzle scenarios such as "Ceres starts with no water and 5% ecology; bring it above 50% using only six buildings". You get a set of finite puzzles with clear finish lines inside the incremental game.
Add a Buy x1 / x10 / Max stepper beside building purchases, with the total cost shown before you click. Late-game shopping gets faster and clearer.
Add interface colour themes named after worlds (Mars rust, Venus amber, Neptune blue), each unlocked when you finish that world. You get a cosmetic reward for every world you complete.

Add relief requests: small outposts and stranded stations ask for a one-off shipment (for example "Pluto Station needs Water Ice"), the request waits as long as you like, and thanks arrive as a friendly log line and a small permanent perk. This fits your helper role, and nothing is lost if you ignore a request.

Add a Wonders catalogue of about 40 named sights (Olympus Mons, the Great Red Spot, Saturn's rings and so on), each unlocked by something you do and shown as a small low-poly card with a short fact read live from NASA's solar system pages. This gives you a collection to fill, with a clear percent complete.

Add three ways to finish the system (Hands-on miner, Trade baron, Hands-off overseer), each with its own ladder of goals and a badge, so the same game can be 100% completed by different play styles. This follows your taste for many ways to play inside one game.

Add a quiet maintenance robot on each world that keeps a short log in a plain, tired voice and has made one mistake early on that it never quite lives down. It gives the game the broken-but-gentle character you like, and its log fills in as you play.

Add a Window Seat view: a slow, dark, low-poly model of the solar system where your Governors run things and a one-line log scrolls by, meant to leave on a second screen. It is your calm watch mode and ends with a friendly "while you were looking" summary.

Add a "this sitting" suggestion at the start: pick Quick (about 15 minutes) or Long, and it offers three small goals sized for that, in any order, with no penalty for ignoring them. You get a clear target for a short session and finish with a win.

Add a number shelf: each named size (million, billion, trillion and beyond) earns a small plaque and a one-line note when your totals first reach it. This feeds your love of huge numbers and the shelf-style collection you like.
Add an "Ask the Governor" button that asks "Would you like a suggestion?" and only then shows one next step, which you can dismiss. This follows your wish that hints must be agreed to first.

Add an express opening: the first world is taught by playing and the second system opens within five minutes, with a gentle ramp-up after that. This follows your wish to start simple and speed up quickly.

Add six riddle achievements whose descriptions are short cryptic lines about places in the system, never a bare "?". This follows your taste for cryptic-but-not-blank hidden achievements and exploration.

Add a build sticker album with one page per world and a sticker for every building, route and ship you have made, plus a percent bar for the whole album. This is the shelf or sticker-book collection style you prefer.

Add a huge Mastery web with many branches that you grow through achievements and exploration, never through resets, and with no refunds. This follows your wish for a huge skill tree and no forced prestige.
Add a mission overlay: one key opens a pop-over list of your current goals over the game and closes again. This is the mission-style progress view you pointed to.
Rename every button in SOL to one clear word. This follows your preference for one-word labels over icons or long phrases.

Add a dark-background colour set with lighter tints for every resource colour, plus a short page explaining the colour choices. This follows your note that dark colour variants are hard to read on dark screens.
Add a pack of 40 dry, dark one-liners for the Governors and the captain's log, never about harm to oneself. This follows your taste for dry, dark humour and your rule on what never to joke about.

Add a radio side story: you are someone who tinkers with radios and picks up a strange signal from an outpost, and you advise its operator through branching choices at your own pace. This follows your Lifeline-style story taste and the radio-tinkerer role, and it is entirely optional.
Add a misunderstood rival AI called the Warden that once helped the system and now seems cold, with log lines that slowly show why. This follows your fondness for tragic, quietly broken characters.
Add a two-player split: you and a friend each run half of the worlds and ship goods across by invite link, with no chat. This follows your wish for optional friend ties and co-op puzzle play.

Add a rescue plan for when ecology collapses and production halts: a named three-step plan that restores output, shown in a clear panel. This follows your wish that a failure should offer a way to restore, never a restart.
Add a mission control skin with green-on-black readouts and an old-computer feel, optional in Settings. This follows your love of space stations and old computers.
Add Other Stars: play a made-up planetary system from a short seed name, replayable and shareable by name. This follows your preference for seeded layouts you can replay.

Add a break-it area in the post-game sandbox where you can push numbers to absurd values, and the log records every funny breakage. This follows your enjoyment of watching glitch hunting and breaking games.

Add colony tales: short three-sentence stories written from your own log (the day the Belt ran dry, the year Venus turned green) that you collect in a book. This follows your enjoyment of watching colony games and a notebook you fill in.

Add mystery signals: a world shows odd instrument readings, you check three instruments, and you name the cause to unlock a bonus. This follows your investigation-and-deduction taste (the Phasmophobia mindset).

Add transfer windows: moving between worlds uses a simple fuel and timing puzzle with distances read live from a named source such as NASA. This follows your interest in Kerbal-style space planning and physics.
Add an orbit maths puzzle that asks you to size a shipment with a quick ratio sum, with a bonus when you are right. This follows your interest in maths, and the puzzle visibly feeds your totals.
Add a recipe book, handed to you, showing every conversion chain (Ice to Water to Fuel) with a tick when you have made it. This follows your preference for handed recipes and your chemistry interest.
Add a tidy base mode where you arrange buildings on each world's map for small neatness bonuses, in a calm, no-pressure way. This follows your liking for the calm of tidy-up games.
Add a pen-pal planet: a friend's finished system appears as a distant trading partner that sends one small gift each visit. This follows your wish for optional friend ties with no chat.
Let every SOL hotkey (pause, speed, each window) be rebound in a Controls tab in Settings by clicking an action and pressing a new key, with clashes flagged. You get keys that fit your own hand.
Let windows such as Overview, Governor Report and Build Plan snap to the screen edges as resizable docked panels that stay open while you play. You can watch every world at once on a wide monitor.
Show a hover card on any resource number with its income per second split by source and a 60-second mini graph. You get the detail without opening a window.
Add a right-click menu on a building with Pin to Build Plan, Show in Chain Reactions and Copy its numbers. You get quick actions with no window hunting.
Add a Ctrl+K command palette where typing "mars" or "regolith" jumps to that world, window, setting or research node. You reach anything in two keystrokes.
Let the number keys 1 to 9 jump the main view to each world in unlock order, and Tab cycle through them. You can move round the system with no mouse.
Make the Overview a real star chart with mouse-wheel zoom, drag to pan, and a click on a world that opens its panel beside the map. You get a proper map on a big monitor.
On screens wider than 1600px, keep the captain's log open as a tall side strip that shows the last 30 lines instead of one. A wide monitor shows the history for free.
Turn the save slots into a file-style load screen listing play time, worlds finished and a tiny skyline for each slot, with rename and duplicate. Loading feels like a real PC game's menu.
Let you save a window layout as "Mining" or "Research" and flip between layouts with F1 and F2. Different sittings get different screens.
Make the main screen a portrait world carousel where you swipe sideways between worlds, each a full-height card with big Buy buttons at the bottom. One thumb can walk the whole system.
Open a bottom sheet with a building's numbers and a Buy button when you long-press it. You get detail without leaving the list.
Restore the exact world, scroll position and open panel when you reopen SOL, with a small "back where you were" chip. A two-minute visit never loses your place.
Add an optional tiny haptic buzz when a purchase lands or a world finishes terraforming, off by default and set in Settings, where the browser allows. Progress becomes something you feel.
Show a one-card summary page when the installed app opens, with worlds finished, your next goal and income per second, before the full game loads. You can check in at a glance during class.
Add a battery-saver calm mode that stops all animation, updates numbers once a second and dims to a dark flat theme while the sim keeps running. Your phone lasts through a long lesson.
Open the Governor Report when you pull down on the main screen. A one-thumb gesture gets you the summary.
Let you swipe a research card right to add it to the Build Plan. You can queue a plan without typing or menus.
When the phone turns sideways, show the Overview beside the current world instead of stacking them. Landscape becomes a two-pane view.
Add a compact number mode with a larger digit size and the unit on a second line (4.2 on top, million below). Big numbers stay readable on a 360px screen.
Add a river across the forest: plots next to the water grow faster, and clearing upstream plots dries out the ones downstream. You see how one decision travels across the map.
Add access roads: clearing plots that touch a road is cheaper, but each road splits the forest and lowers wildlife counts on both sides. You get a real spatial trade-off to plan around.
Add natural regrowth: a bare plot beside three or more mature plots slowly recovers for free, with visible drifting seeds. You see that protecting an intact core helps the whole forest heal.

Add two new regions, a boreal forest and a tropical rainforest, each with its own growth speed, wildlife list and one main real-world cause of loss with a named source. You get fresh maps to replay with different rhythms.
Add a meadow strip option for a cleared plot: a cheap, quick habitat that earns a little biodiversity but little timber value. You get a middle path between clearing and full replanting.
Add a paint tool: pick Clear, Replant or Adopt, then drag across many plots to apply it. Big forests become quick to manage.
Show a projected outcome on each stakeholder request ("accepting changes your value by about -40 over 10 seasons") before you choose. You can make informed choices instead of guessing.
Add a carbon readout that converts your standing forest into tonnes of CO2 stored, using a per-hectare figure read live from a named source. You see your forest's size in real-world terms.
Extend undo to replant and preserve actions as well as clearing, for a short time. Misclicks stop being costly.
Add an age overlay that tints each plot by how old its trees are, with the age printed on it. You can spot which parts of the forest are fragile young growth.
Show tree rings when you tap a mature plot: one ring per season it has survived, with a notch for each nearby clearing. You get a quiet, readable history of each plot.

Add a season-matched replanting bonus: seedlings planted in the right season establish faster, and the season strip hints at the best moment. You get a small planning choice that rewards paying attention.
Show a payback line on every clear action: how many seasons until replanting that plot would have beaten the quick income. You learn the long game at the exact moment you decide.
Add a short fact card for each wildlife species in the log, with its conservation status read live from a named source such as the IUCN Red List. The wildlife log becomes something worth reading.
Add twin forests: a second small forest beside the first, where mature plots along the shared border let animals cross and boost both sides. You get a bigger-picture mode about connected habitat.

Add wildlife rescue: when you clear a plot, displaced animals appear and you can carry them to a mature plot by tapping both, earning a shelter badge for each species. This is a gentle healer role with no failure state.

Add a Night Forest look: a dark low-poly version of the grid where fireflies, owls and bats appear and eight new night animals join the wildlife log. It gives you a moody look and a new collection to complete.

Add a Quiet Grove calm mode: no requests, no events, just tending and watching the forest grow, with the same progress counting toward your totals. It is a relaxed mode where progress can never be lost.
Add a Dome Garden level set on Mars: the same forest rules with thin soil, a sealed dome and strange hardy wildlife. It brings your space and science fiction taste into the forest.

Add a Valley Map where each short forest you finish (about five minutes) restores one patch of a large painted valley, and the full map shows every patch. Short wins build one bigger picture you can see.
Add three ways to master the forest (Ranger, Naturalist, Planner), each with its own list of goals and badge so you can reach 100% in different ways. This gives you the many-ways-to-play feel.
Add forest fog: unexplored plots start hidden in mist and clear as you tend their neighbours, though fog never stops play. This follows your dark foggy-forest taste and exploration.
Add forest floor finds: tending mature plots reveals 30 small things (fungi, feathers, old tools) that go on a shelf. This follows your "one of everything" collecting habit.
Add a ranger's field notebook drawn in a rough hand-sketched look that fills with sketches as you discover things. This follows your liking for hand-drawn art and a notebook you fill in.
Add a Gothic Hollow level: twisted dark woods with ravens and lantern light, using the same rules. This follows your dark, moody and gothic taste.
Add a branching story where you steer a ranger who made a costly mistake years ago and must decide how to face it. This follows your Lifeline-style story taste and your rule against all-good heroes.
Add farmer partners: neighbouring farmers ask you to plan hedgerows and tree lines on their land, and each has their own view. This follows your helper role and the multiple-viewpoints rule.
Add a shared grove: two friends tend one forest by invite link, each owning half the plots and sending help across the border. This follows your wish for optional friend ties and co-op play.
Add a low-poly 3D view of the forest you can rotate, alongside the flat grid. This follows your low-poly taste and your wish for scenes over charts.
Add an Explorer family of ten achievements for trying every kind of action, season and plot state. This follows your preference for exploration and completion achievements.
Add a routine card where you pick three chores (water, tend, check wildlife) shown as a strip you tick each visit. This follows your preference for a calm routine you know by heart.
Add a mystery of the dying plot: you check soil, camera trap and water samples and name the cause. This follows your investigation and deduction taste.

Add grove puzzles: stone panels hidden in the forest ask you to plant tree lines that satisfy clues, with every solved panel unlocking something. This follows your love of spatial and logic puzzles with an intricate Witness-style depth.
Add a silent stag companion that follows the pointer and shows feelings with its posture, never words. This follows your liking for wordless companions that show emotion.
Add a cabin in the woods: a side-view cutaway of a little cabin that you furnish with the things you find. This follows your dream game's cabin and cutaway views.
Add a carbon balance puzzle: match what a plot takes in and gives out to earn a growth boost. This follows your maths and chemistry interest, and the result visibly counts.
Add a drone surveyor, a small low-poly robot that scans plots and fills a scan log. This follows your robot and computers taste.
Add camera traps: frame a shot of each animal for a photo album. This follows your collecting habit and the photo taste.
Add three voices: short branching days as a logger, a ranger and a landowner who each see the same forest differently. This follows your wish for several points of view.
Add a guided ramp where new tools appear every few minutes of play during the first half hour. This follows your wish to start simple and then pick up fast.
Add seed merging: three matching seedlings combine into a rarer kind, with no timers or energy. This follows your liking for merge games without their timers.
Give adopted trees favourites and dislikes that they hint at, with small gifts (water, mulch) raising their friendship for perks. This follows your dream-game friendship and gift ideas.
Add a forager's recipe book, handed to you, for turning finds into tea, lantern oil and more for the cabin. This follows your preference for handed recipes and collecting.
Add forest anomalies: two photos of the same plot with one change, which you spot and file in a catalogue. This follows your taste for anomaly-style games.
Add a cross-section view of one plot showing roots, soil layers and burrows. This follows your wish for cutaway views and pictures over charts.
Show a hover card on a plot with its tree age, income per tick, recovery stage and what a click would do. You read a plot without clicking it.
Add mouse-wheel zoom, drag panning and a corner minimap that shows plot health on big forests. You can manage a large grid from one screen.
Add a right-click menu on a plot with Tend, Golden seedling, Clear, Replant, Adopt and Inspect, each showing its hotkey. You learn the keys by using the mouse.
Let Ctrl+1 to Ctrl+4 save named cursor spots (for example "the poacher edge") and 1 to 4 jump back to them. You can hop between trouble areas in one key.
Pin the Ranger contracts as a permanent right-hand tray whose lines jump the cursor to the requested plot when clicked. Contracts stay in view while you work.
Add a seasons scrub bar under the forest that you drag to replay how the grid changed over the last 20 seasons. You see your forest grow back like a time-lapse.
Add a Controls tab in Settings that lists all twelve Canopy keys and lets you rebind each one. You can move the cursor and tend plots with your own layout.
Let you drag a plot onto the Seed Vault tray to store its seedling and drag a stored seed back to a bare plot. Moving seeds feels like handling real objects.
When the window is wider than 1700px, show income, biodiversity and relations as three stacked live graphs in the side column. Big screens show trends at a glance.
Show a faint ring on the grid cursor with an arrow-key trail of where it has been this minute. You can see which plots you keep missing.
Make the forest fill a portrait screen with plots sized for thumbs, so a pinch zooms the grid and a two-finger drag moves it. A big forest stays playable on a phone.
Let a swipe across a row of plots queue Tend on each plot you touch. One finger waters a whole row.
Add an optional light buzz when a plot is replanted or a golden seedling is caught, where the browser allows. Good actions feel solid under your thumb.
Reopen Canopy on the exact plot you last selected, with its bottom sheet already open if it was. Short sessions pick up at once.
Put the three most useful buttons (Tend, Golden, Replant) in a thumb arc at the bottom right and let you swap sides for left-handed play. One hand reaches everything.
Show a home-screen summary card with standing value, forest health and the next contract on opening the installed app. You can check the forest before the game boots.
Add a calm bed-time forest mode that dims to a slow dark canopy, hides numbers except one, and lets the forest pass seasons quietly while you watch. A tired player still gets a pleasant screen.
Make the poacher alert a large edge-of-screen banner you can swipe away or tap to drive them off. A phone player can respond with one touch.
Collapse each side panel into a bottom tab strip with icons (Plots, Contracts, Vault, Almanac) that you swipe between. You get card-sized screens instead of one long scroll.
Add pull-down on the forest to run a quick Tend All with a short summary of what changed. A one-gesture upkeep pass fits a two-minute visit.

Add city growth that includes electrifying transport and heating, so demand jumps are announced as stories ("Bus fleets go electric in 3 rounds"). You learn why clean power matters for more than lights.
Announce big new demand a few rounds ahead ("A data centre opens in 3 rounds, +40 demand"). You can plan builds instead of being surprised.
Add transmission lines: plants far from the city can only deliver fully if you build and pay for lines. You get a planning puzzle about where power is made versus used.
Add a winter and summer split to each round, because summer air conditioning and winter heating create different peaks that different plants cover best. You see why one plant type is never enough.
Add community consultation when you build: residents voice different views (jobs, noise, safety, view) and you pick a compensation option. You see several points of view on every plant.
Add repowering: convert an old coal plant into a gas or biomass plant for a fee instead of fully retiring it. You get a middle option and a taste of how real utilities decide.
Add a carbon capture retrofit for fossil plants, with a short note giving the arguments for and against it. You get a debated option to weigh yourself.
Add community solar: buy rooftop solar in tiny increments that trickle in capacity. You get a low-risk way to start renewables with a small budget.
Add a household bill meter showing the average electricity bill and how it affects lower-income households. You see that a good grid is also an affordable one.

Show each plant's nameplate capacity next to what it really delivers on average, with the typical figures read live from a named source such as the US Energy Information Administration. You learn why a 100 MW solar farm is not 100 MW all day.
Add legacy cost notes when you retire a plant (ash, waste, site cleanup) as a small recurring line. You see costs that last past a plant's life.
Add a beginner view that hides advanced rows until you have built your first battery and first renewable. New players get a calm screen and veterans can switch it off.

Add a learning-curve chart showing how your renewable costs fell with what you built, beside the real historical solar price curve read live from a named source such as Our World in Data. You see that the game's cost drop matches real life.
Add a fleet age timeline: a bar showing when each plant reaches the end of its life across the next rounds. You can see a retirement cliff coming and plan for it.
Add a note to self: write one line at the end of a round and see it at the start of the next. You keep your plan in mind across a long run.

Add a control room terminal: a dark console where you can type short commands such as "build solar 2" or "advance 3" as an alternative to buttons. It suits your computers-and-code taste and is a second way to play.

Add a work orders board with three open jobs at all times ("Reach 40% clean", "Build 2 batteries", "Go 3 rounds with no brownout"), done in any order, each unlocking something when finished. You always have three goals in view and no strict order.

Add Incident Files: every kind of disruption gets a file the first time you handle it, with what caused it and what stops it, and a completion percent. This gives you a collection to fill that doubles as the lesson.

Add an island rescue scenario: a remote island has lost power after a storm and you rebuild its grid from scratch, with islanders, fishers and the clinic each voicing what they need. It is a helper story that shows several points of view.

Add three operator styles (Engineer, Economist, Campaigner) that change which numbers the dashboard highlights and which perks you earn, each with its own badge to complete. You get many ways to play inside one game.
Add a clever-solution badge for finishing a scenario with the cheapest or neatest plan, not the fastest. This follows your preference for rewarding clever over fast.

Add a two-operator mode where one friend runs supply and the other runs demand programmes, each seeing different screens and talking it out. This follows your Keep Talking enjoyment and co-op puzzle idea.
Add a blackout restore sequence: after a big outage you rebuild in a named order with a clear ending, so no run is lost. This follows your wish that a failure should offer a way to restore.
After three bad rounds in a row, offer a "would you like help?" button that eases demand or gives a hint, never forced. This follows your wish for an offer of easier play after repeated failures.
Add line-crew robots you name and upgrade that handle maintenance on plants. This follows your robot taste.
Add a Moon base scenario powering a colony through long lunar nights, with the day length read live from a named source such as NASA. This follows your space and sci-fi taste.
Add a Brownout City story scenario in a dark dystopian city that rations power by district, played from several residents' views. This follows your dystopia taste and the multiple-viewpoints rule.
Add a priority list for shortages (hospital, school, homes, factory) with the consequences explained in plain words. This follows your care about healthcare and housing.

Add a parts catalogue of 40 components (turbines, panels, transformers) with specs read live from a named source such as the US Energy Information Administration. This follows your collect-one-of-everything habit.
Add amber and green phosphor display themes for a retro control room. This follows your old computers and dark colour taste.
Add a silent droid called Spark that shows feelings with lights and never speaks. This follows your wordless droid companion idea.
Add fault tracing: a flicker happens, you check three instruments, and you name the cause for a bonus. This follows your deduction and investigation taste.
Add rule-tile puzzles where grid rules are words you rearrange ("coal costs double", "wind pays more") to reach a goal. This follows your love of Baba Is You style puzzles.
Add own-best bars for cost, emissions and rounds on each scenario so you can beat yourself without ranking against anyone. This follows your preference for optimising without competing.
Add equippable parts for each plant, three slots each, with fixed unlocks from milestones (no random drops). This follows your looter-style taste without luck.
Add a neon-on-black Tron-style skin with glowing lines. This follows your Tron fandom and dark look.
Add a Continental Grid endgame where several regions run together and numbers reach billions. This follows your love of huge exponential growth.
Add a hand-drawn blueprint look for plant pictures. This follows your occasional liking for hand-drawn art.
Add spare capacity favours: a friend's grid can send you one gift of spare capacity, and you can send one back. This follows your helper role and optional friend ties.
Add a physics bench where you adjust voltage, current and distance to see why power is lost in wires. This follows your physics interest.
Add unit conversion mini-puzzles (kW, MW, GW) that give a small funds bonus when right. This follows your maths interest, and the puzzle visibly counts.
Add script puzzles where you write the shortest set of if-then rules that survive a storm. This follows your wish to learn coding through puzzles.
Add a household story following one family across the run through branching choices about bills and heating. This follows your Lifeline-style story taste and your housing concerns.
Add a haunted substation scenario with odd readings you must explain, with no jump scares. This follows your liking for anomaly and eerie games.
Add commentated runs: a step-by-step expert run with a text commentary track you can step through or let play. This follows your enjoyment of long, commented let's plays.
Let you drag plants from a parts bin straight onto a grid map and drag them off to retire them, with the cost shown as you hover. Building a power system feels like a real tycoon game.
Show a hover card on each plant with output, cost, emissions and its learning-curve price after your next build. You compare options without a calculation.
Add a right-click menu on a plant to Upgrade, Retire, Pin to the plan and Show in the weather log. Common jobs sit one click from the plant.
Add a live demand-versus-supply chart that fills the centre of a wide screen and shows next round's forecast as a dashed line. You see shortfalls coming on a big display.
Let number keys 1 to 6 pick plant types and Enter build the selected one, with Backspace to retire. You can play a whole round from the keyboard.
Let you save window layouts such as "Planner" (chart, plants and weather log) and "Review" (summary and career), switched with F1 and F2. The screen fits the task.
Add a bottom bar of F1 to F8 labelled keys (Build, Retire, Advance, Chart, Weather, Career and more) that works by key or click. Mouse and keyboard players share one clear control strip.

Add a wide Plan Table window where every plant is a row with sortable columns for cost, output, emissions and payback, and a click in a row builds one. You can optimise like a spreadsheet inside the game.
Add a draggable what-if slider for the next round's weather variability that redraws the forecast chart as you move it. You test how risky a mix is before committing.
Add a compare-to-last-run strip under the chart that shows your previous run's mix as a ghost outline. You can see at once whether you are doing better.
Make the plant list a vertical stack of large cards where a swipe right builds one and each card shows its price change. Managing the grid works with one thumb.
Pin round, funds and the supply-versus-demand gap in a thin top strip that turns bold when demand outruns supply. You see the main number without scrolling.
Let you drag a finger along the demand chart to read each round's supply and demand in a floating bubble. You read the chart by touch.
Show a warning chip when forecast demand exceeds supply that opens a sheet of fixes when tapped. A problem comes with a one-tap path to solve it.
Add a card density option (compact, normal, roomy) in Settings. The plant cards fit your phone and your eyes.
Show an installed-app home card with the current round, emissions trend and a "next best build" line before the game opens. You can glance at your grid in class.
Add a half-asleep Auto-plan that suggests one build per round as a big single button and shows the effect in plain words. A tired player can still make steady progress.
Turn the weather log into a horizontal card strip you swipe through, one card per round. Reading the past is a thumb flick.
Show emissions as a thin line along the top edge that fills across the screen as they grow. The long-term goal is visible without a panel.
Let a long-press on any gauge pop up a bottom sheet with a plain-words explanation and its last five values. You get the detail without a hover.
Add a fishing quota dial: set how much you catch each season against the fish stock. You learn overfishing as a separate pressure from acidity.
Add managed retreat: you can deliberately move the lowest row inland, with residents, farmers and the council each reacting differently. You face a hard real-world choice from several points of view.
Add a town meeting every five seasons where three groups argue for different plans and you choose a compromise. You see how a community actually decides.
Add seaweed farms that soak up some acidity locally but cost upkeep. You get a new, researched way to fight acidification besides spending points.
Add a hatchery industry whose young die at lower acidity than adult fish, acting as an early warning. You learn how some businesses feel ocean change first.
Add king tide seasons that are shown in advance and make storm surges worse when they overlap. You get a sensible reason to prepare for particular seasons.
Add zoning: ban new homes on the lowest row to cut future damage at the cost of slower growth. You see the trade-off real planners face.
Add beach nourishment: pay to restore a lost shore row for a few seasons, repeatable. You get a short-term fix that teaches why it is not permanent.
Add storm drains and pumps as a defence against rain flooding, separate from the seawall. You learn that floods have more than one cause.
Add a tidal power plant option whose income follows the tide cycle. You get a clean energy choice that fits the seaside setting.

Add a sea-level pathway picker (low, middle, high) using published scenario names and numbers read live from a named source such as the IPCC. You can play against the future you choose and see where the numbers come from.
Add a money flow view showing where each season's funds go (fishing, upkeep, walls, reduction). You can see at once what is eating your budget.
Add a pH explainer that shows acidity as a pH number and a small slider demonstrating that each step is a tenfold change. You finally see why a small number change is a big deal.
Give each heritage site a short, invented three-line history that is revealed when you protect it. Saving a site feels like saving a story, not a tile.
Add a small coastline preview for each scenario on the start screen showing its rows, walls and starting risks. You can choose a scenario knowing what you are getting.
Add Lighthouse Night: a dark, low-poly night harbour with a lighthouse beam, and the water glowing a stranger blue as acidity climbs. It gives you the creepy ocean tone you like.

Add rescue boats: in storm seasons, boats call for help and you choose which harbour gate or light to open for them, with nobody lost on screen and a "restore and try again" if you misjudge. This gives you a helper role.

Add Specimen Jars: unusual deep-water creatures that appear as the ocean changes, each stored in a jar on a shelf with a short fact read live from a named source such as the World Register of Marine Species. You get a creepy-but-calm collection to complete.
Add a survey robot you can send to scan one stretch of sea and reveal its acidity, with twelve buoy sites to place and collect. It is a robot helper with a clear collection goal.
Add a Harbor Charter board with three standing goals (Seawall level 5, Reef level 5, Fleet level 5), each unlocking a named upgrade, done in any order. You always see three goals and no strict route.
Add sea fog that hides distant rows until buoys or the lighthouse reveal them. This follows your dark foggy taste and exploration.
Add a marine radio story with branching replies to fishers and a lighthouse keeper with a secret, told at your own pace. This follows your Lifeline-style story taste.
Let a friend's saved harbour become your sister settlement so you can compare choices with no chat. This follows your optional friend ties.

Add the Warden Engine, a seawall automaton that once saved the town and is now blamed for floods, and let you decide how to treat it. This follows your fondness for tragic, misunderstood savior characters.
Add harbour mysteries (lights under water, empty boats) that you solve from tide logs by naming the cause. This follows your deduction and eerie taste.
Add a shell shelf of 30 shells that wash up after storms by storm type, with no randomness. This follows your collecting habit.
Add a wave physics bench where you stack tide and surge waves to see why they combine. This follows your maths and physics interest.
Add an acid balance puzzle that rebalances carbonate pieces on a board for a one-off boost. This follows your chemistry interest.
Add drain lines, a Flow-Free-style puzzle that routes floodwater out of town, lowering the next storm's damage. This follows your Flow Free fondness, and it visibly counts.
Add a harbour cross-section showing seabed, pilings, pipes and fish in layers. This follows your dream game's cutaway views.
Add a Europa dome harbour scenario under an icy moon's surface. This follows your space and dark-ocean taste.
Add a salvage beach where you sort washed-up objects onto a shelf in a calm puzzle. This follows your liking for the calm of tidy-up games.
Add a harbour saboteur puzzle where you find who is secretly overfishing from catch records. This follows your Among Us and deduction taste.
Add a harbour watch screen that runs your saved plan through a slow sunrise-to-sunset time-lapse. This follows your calm watch mode taste.
Add a hand-drawn nautical chart look with a compass rose. This follows your occasional liking for hand-drawn art.
Add bottle messages: you can send a friend a bottle with a shell and a picked icon note. This follows your wish for gifts and notes with no chat.
Add wreck sites revealed by survey, each with three salvage items to collect. This follows your creepy ocean and collecting taste.
Give harbour residents favourite and hated things they hint at, with small gifts raising friendship for perks. This follows your dream-game friendship idea.
Add chart-reading puzzles that use bearings and soundings to place a lighthouse. This follows your spatial puzzle and maths taste.
Add a boatyard where you sort parts to restore old boats, each joining a shelf with the last captain's quiet log. This follows your restoring-machines idea.
Add a lighthouse lens puzzle where mirrors and prisms steer the beam. This follows your spatial puzzle taste.
Add a tide routine, a fixed three-step harbour round you can do by heart each season. This follows your preference for a calm routine.
Add signal flag decoding puzzles that unlock messages. This follows your code and cipher interest.
Add a low-poly 3D coast you can rotate with water rising visibly. This follows your low-poly taste.
Add a tidal turbine gear puzzle where you fit gears to turn a tidal turbine. This follows your tinkering and spatial taste.
Draw the harbour as a wide scene where you click a stretch of coast to place a seawall or wetland and see its flood protection range as you hover. Adaptation becomes a map you edit.
Add a hover crosshair on the sea-level and acidity graphs that shows the exact season, value and which of your choices drove it. You can read the delay between cause and effect directly.
Add a right-click menu on the coastline with Build seawall, Restore wetland, Inspect and Add to the planner. You reach the choices from the map.
Let you resize the Season Planner window and pin it beside the harbour scene while you play. You can edit the plan and watch the result together.
Add a Pin button on each graph that floats it as a small always-on-top window beside the scene. You watch acidity or sea level while you work.
Add a dual-view pane that shows the coastline "then" and "now" side by side with a draggable divider that wipes between them. You can see how much the sea has taken in one gesture.
Let a middle-click on a coast section toggle between seawall and wetland previews. Comparing defences is fast.
Show season history as a filmstrip under the scene so a click on any frame displays the harbour as it was. You can browse your timeline like a video editor.
Let you save planner layouts as named "plans" that you load from a dropdown and compare with the current one in a split view. You can try two strategies without losing either.
On wide screens, keep the Harbor Ledger open as a right-hand table that auto-scrolls to the newest season. A permanent record sits next to the action.
Turn the harbour scene into a full-width portrait view where you drag a seawall icon onto the coast and release to place it. Adapting the coast is a direct touch.
Keep Advance Season as a large button at the bottom centre with a ring showing seasons left in the year. The main action sits under your thumb.
Keep a slim sea-level gauge on the screen edge with the flood line marked. The main danger stays visible while you scroll.
Zoom the harbour into the stretch of coast you are protecting with a double-tap. Detail is one gesture away.
Show a swipeable season strip at the top with tiny bars for each season's income and sea level, and a tap to open one. History is a flick.
Show the three meters as large swipeable cards that fit one screen each, with the graph on the back of each card. You read one thing at a time.
Add a calm harbour mode that dims the scene, slows the water, and hides all numbers except a single health word. It suits playing in bed half asleep.
Let you tap and hold a season on the graph to see what you decided then in a bottom sheet. History is a thumb away.
Add a battery-saver toggle that stops the waves and cloud movement and redraws only when you advance. The game stops draining your phone.
Make invest buttons a vertical thumb rail on the right edge, with a flip to the left for left-handers. The most-used controls are in reach.
Add a recovery phase after each event where you choose what to repair first (homes, power, food) with a clear cost for each. You get a meaningful decision after the shock, not just before it.
Add drills: spend a little to practise for a named upcoming event type and soften its damage a bit. You get a cheap, readable way to prepare.
Add an emergency stockpile you fill from your growth that cushions a later event, with no spoilage. You can save for rainy days on purpose.
Show knock-on arrows after an event (a flood leads to illness next, a heatwave to power strain). You see how one disaster feeds the next.

Add case file runs, each built around a real disaster sequence with its events and outcomes read live from a named source, with the responders' different views listed. You learn from real events as a playable challenge.
Add doctrines chosen at the start of a run (Fortify, Evacuate, Rebuild) that tilt how your skills perform. You get distinct styles to try on the same schedule.
Add a "what if I had..." button after a run that replays the same events with a different split of resources. You learn which choice mattered most.
Add a risk radar chart comparing how exposed you are to each kind of event with how covered you are. You can see your weak side before the next event arrives.
Add shelter capacity versus population as a visible number that limits how much harm evacuations can prevent. You see a practical limit real planners work with.
Add a "who pays?" choice after big events (taxes, aid, loans), with each option judged differently by three groups of citizens. You see the trade-offs behind recovery funding.
Add short milestone screens that explain what the real-world equivalent of your best defence is, with the example read live from a named source. You connect a game win to something real people did.
