Add a preparedness checklist for each event type with real household and community tips read live from a named source such as the Red Cross or FEMA. You get a practical takeaway for each kind of shock.
Add four more event types (drought, wildfire, landslide, cold snap, skipping any already in the game), each with its own best defences. The tree gets more to think about and runs feel fresh.
Add a post-run ribbon showing every event in order with a shield or crack mark for how it went. You can read the shape of your run at a glance.
Show a difficulty rating on each scenario drawn from anonymous community runs (hidden until enough runs exist). You can pick a challenge that suits you.
Add an event lab: test your current tree against any one event at any strength, with the result shown and nothing saved to your run. You can try ideas safely before a real run.
Add scenario flavour text with local place names, wording and event descriptions for each setting (harbour, farmland, hill town). Each setting reads like its own place.
After each event, show two contrasting real responses to a similar disaster, each with its source and its critics, read live from a named source. You see that recovery choices are argued about.
Add a Defence Only mode with fixed income where you manage defences and repairs as a pure puzzle. It gives you a calmer, more planned way to play.
Add a Rebuild start: the run begins with the settlement already damaged by a big event, and you recover before the next one arrives. It fits the game's name and gives a new kind of opening.

Add relief convoys: after an event you can send some of your resources to a neighbouring settlement run by the computer, and it sends back help in a later run. It fits your helper role and costs you only what you choose to give.

Add a field clinic puzzle after heatwaves: sort simple cases with limited supplies, nobody dies on screen, and a bad plan simply lets you retry. It is a healer role, and its result feeds your recovery so the minigame always counts.
Add a Memento Cabinet: each kind of event you survive leaves a small keepsake (a flood marker, a lantern, a stuck clock) in a low-poly cabinet. You get a collection with a clear percent complete.

Add a Night After view: a dark low-poly settlement where every lit window is a household that came through safe, so your result looks like a glowing town. It gives you a moody picture of what your choices saved.
Add a Marathon mode of 40 events across a long timeline, with save anywhere and no pressure, for those over-three-hours evenings. It gives you a long, optional way to play.
Add three resilience goals shown at all times, each "get this branch of the tree to level 5 to unlock that", in any order. You always know what to work on next.
Add a disaster hotline: Lifeline-style branching messages where you advise a survivor, kept gentle with no scenes of self-harm. This follows your Lifeline taste and helper role.
Add Two Towns: two friends each run a settlement in the same valley and can lend resources once between events, with no chat. This follows your optional friend ties and mutual aid idea.
Add an after-event investigation where you read three records and name why a defence failed, earning a skill discount. This follows your deduction taste.
Add 60 survivor letters, short and dry but kind, each unlocked by a specific achievement and kept in a notebook. This follows your notebook-style lore taste.
Add a storm cellar cutaway showing a dark cross-section of the settlement and its shelters. This follows your cutaway and dark-look taste.
Add a Mars habitat scenario with dust storms, hull breaches and power loss. This follows your space and science-fiction taste.
Add rescue robots you unlock as skills, each named and quietly expressive, that search after events. This follows your robot taste and wordless-companion idea.
Add evacuation puzzles where you place signs and barriers so everyone reaches shelter by one route. This follows your spatial puzzle taste, and it visibly feeds evacuation results.
Add a water test kit where you read strips and decide boil, treat or discard. This follows your chemistry interest and care about access to water.
Add an early-warning AI character with dry, caring lines, a bit like a facility computer you cannot stay annoyed with. This follows your Portal 2 character taste.
Add a tidy-up puzzle in the recovery phase where you sort belongings back into homes. This follows your liking for calm tidy-up games.

Add a Pocket Aftermath run of three events in about five minutes with its own small tree that feeds into the main one. This follows your short-wins-into-a-bigger-picture taste and sub-20-minute sessions.
Add a short animated recap of each event, four hand-drawn-style panels built from what happened. This follows your preference for short animations and pictures over charts.
Add an atlas map that fills in as you finish each scenario, with a percent bar. This follows your percent-bar and map-filling preference.
Add Relief Coordinator mode, where you play the aid organisation deciding where limited teams go among four towns, with no deaths on screen. This follows your helper role and rights concerns.
Add a barrier design puzzle where you place blocks to hold back a water line and the stable ones become permanent options. This follows your physics and spatial puzzle taste.
Add scavenging expeditions where you send a team to a ruin, with the outcomes shown beforehand so there is no luck. This follows your preference for predictability and looting.
Add a rubble search scene where you click to find supplies and survivors. This follows your first-person helping-nodes idea.
Add a dry news ticker with dark headlines that never mock victims. This follows your dry, dark humour taste and your rule on what never to joke about.
Add a strata view where each past run is a layer in a geological cross-section. This follows your pictures-over-charts preference.
Add seasonal looks across a run: orange autumn, bare winter trees and snow. This follows your dream game's season changes.
Add hazard map painting, where you colour zones on a hand-drawn map and are scored on how well you matched the real risk. This follows your spatial planning and hand-drawn taste.

Add a save-the-archive packing puzzle that moves records and artefacts to safety, each saved item entering a heritage catalogue with a sourced note. This follows your history studies and collecting habit.
Add a vulnerability lens that shows who is hit hardest by each event (renters, elderly, disabled) and a policy to protect them. This follows your care about housing, healthcare and equal rights.

Show the skill tree as a pannable, zoomable map with the mouse wheel and a drag, with a hover card on each node showing cost, effect and which runs used it. You can plan your resilience build like in a big PC skill tree.
Add a hotkey bar along the bottom of the run screen with big keys for Invest, Face event and Undo that light up when pressed. The key bindings are visible and easy to learn.
Add a right-click menu on an investment with Pin as a goal, Show linked nodes and Compare with last run. You get quick tools while planning.
Add Ctrl+F search above the skill tree that dims every node except those matching a word like "flood", with Enter to jump to the next match. You find the part of the tree you want at once.
Let you detach the Disaster Codex into a floating window you can resize and keep open during a run. You look up the next event type while you decide.
Add a Past Runs table with sortable columns (date, severity, damage prevented, resilience reached) and a click that opens a run's event ribbon. You can analyse your history like a spreadsheet.
Add a UI scale and density setting (compact, normal, roomy) that resizes every panel together. The game fits a 1080p monitor or a 4K screen.
Keep a strip of up to three pinned skill goals above the tree, each with a progress bar and a click to jump to the node. You always see your next three goals.
Show a hover preview on each upcoming event slot that lists the damage types it is known to bring. You can plan against what you know.
Add a wide-screen dashboard layout with run, tree and codex in three always-open columns above 1800px. A big monitor holds the whole loop at once.
Make each run a stack of event cards that you swipe through, with Invest as a bottom sheet of large buttons. A run plays as a short card-sized session.
Show the coming disaster as a full-width banner card at the top with its icon and a plain word for severity, and let a swipe down expand its codex entry. You see the threat before you spend.
Put the Invest buttons in a bottom sheet with three snap heights (peek, half, full) that you drag between. You choose how much of the run stays visible while you decide.
Add a home-screen card with your resilience level, total knowledge points and the next affordable skill node. You can see where your tree stands at a glance.
Put the skill tree on a vertical scroll of branch cards, each with a locked count and a tap to expand. The big tree fits a thumb.
Add a swipe from a skill node to the left to pin it as a goal. Planning your next unlock is one gesture.
Add a bed-time mode that dims the screen, enlarges buttons and offers one recommended investment per round. A tired player still makes sensible progress.
Let a double-tap on an affordable skill node buy it, with a confirm tick. Unlocking is a gesture.
Pin knowledge points and resilience in a thin top strip that stays visible while you scroll. You keep your main numbers in sight.
Let a long-press on a past run open a bottom sheet with its three biggest lessons. History is readable at phone size.

Add a lever for rotational grazing that improves the pasture and cuts feed costs, with a note giving both supportive and critical views of its climate benefit. You get a realistic option with honest limits.
Add a town hall where a farmer, a regulator, a vegan activist and a shopper each react to your changes. You see the issue from several sides.
Add a feed source choice (cheap imported soy or pricier local feed). You learn how supply chains link farms to forests.
Add a water use meter beside methane, so some choices fix one and worsen the other. You see that a footprint has more than one number.

Add a switch to read methane over 20 years or 100 years, using the conversion factors read live from a named source such as the IPCC. You see why the same cow can look different depending on the time frame.
Add a click-through supply chain for a litre of milk or a kilo of beef that shows methane per step. You learn where the emissions actually come from.
Add a benchmark line comparing your emissions per litre or kilo with real farms, read live from a named source such as the FAO. You see how your farm stacks up.
Add a short-farm variant of 8 rounds with a full report card. You get a quick way to try a new idea.
Add a heat stress lever (shade and cooling) for hot rounds. You get a climate adaptation option on your own farm.
Add silvopasture: planting trees across part of the pasture for shade, carbon and slower income. You get a long-term investment with a visible payoff.
Add a soil health bar fed by your grazing choices. You can watch the land recover.
Add a sheep and goat flock option with its own methane, income and welfare numbers. You get another animal to compare with cattle and poultry.
Add a methane lifetime line showing that methane from ten rounds ago has mostly broken down while carbon dioxide stays. You see why cutting methane works quickly.
Add a side-by-side comparison of any two levers (cost, methane saved, welfare, income). You can choose between close options with the numbers in front of you.
Add farmyard decorating: place barns, fences, trees and signs in your yard purely for looks, with new items unlocked by what you achieve. You get a creative reward for progress.
Add a Field Notebook of wild animals that return as you rewild (hares, owls, bees, frogs), each ticked off the first time it appears. You get a completable collection that rewards good decisions.

Add an Extension Officer role: you advise three computer-run farms on how to decouple, spending your effort on the lever that helps each one most. It is a helper mode where you improve other farms instead of competing.

Add a Night Pasture calm mode: a dark low-poly field under stars where the herd grazes and methane glows as a faint green haze, with only gentle controls. It suits late-night play and counts toward your totals.
Add barn robots (milking robot, feed pusher, methane-sniffer drone) as low-poly upgrades you can collect and watch working. This brings robots and machines into the game.
Add three farm identities (Techie, Naturalist, Dealmaker), each with its own list of goals and badge so every identity can reach 100%. It gives you many ways to play inside one game.
Add a food access view showing how many households your farm feeds and how prices affect poorer families. This follows your care about food access and the multiple-viewpoints rule.
Add a breeding puzzle where you pair animals to reach target traits using simple trait squares. This follows your maths interest and breed collecting.
Add a vet clinic where you diagnose sick animals from symptoms, and a healthy herd lifts welfare. This follows your healer role and deduction taste.
Let a friend's farm use your methane capture unit for a shared bonus on both farms. This follows your optional friend ties.
Add an orbital farm scenario with hydroponics and protein vats, where power and not methane is the constraint. This follows your space taste.
Add a flare-or-capture puzzle where you balance methane and oxygen pieces to see why burning gas beats venting it. This follows your chemistry interest.
Add a leak hunt where you scan the barn with sensors to find leaks, and fixing one gives a capture bonus. This follows your investigation taste.
Add secret combinations of three levers that speed up decoupling dramatically, hinted by cryptic notebook pages. This follows your delight in finding the one broken build.
Add a barn cutaway where you arrange tools and feed on a side-view cross-section for small efficiency gains. This follows your cutaway view taste.
Add a dairy line puzzle where you build a small conveyor line from milk to cheese and improve it. This follows your factory-optimisation taste.
Add dry satirical memos from a head office that pushes growth, which you can follow or resist. This follows your dry humour and Portal 2 corporate character taste.
Give your farmhands favourites and dislikes that they hint at, and small gifts raise friendship for perks. This follows your dream-game friendship idea.
Add a recipe shelf showing the products your farm makes and the dishes they become. This follows your handed-recipes and collecting taste.
Add fence puzzles where you draw fences to enclose the right paddocks, and solved layouts improve your pasture. This follows your spatial puzzle taste.
Add a circular loop puzzle where you route waste back into inputs on a board so nothing is wasted. This follows your optimising and Factorio-curious taste.
Add a grazing route planner on a small map where you plan herd moves to avoid overgrazing. This follows your spatial planning taste.
Add hay stacking, a calm fitting puzzle for storing feed. This follows your calm tidy-up taste.
Add a local newspaper front page built from your session, with a headline and a quote. This follows your digital and social media studies.
Add a spin desk where you choose how to frame your results for different audiences and see how each reads them. This follows your media studies and multiple-viewpoints rule.
Add twelve hidden corners in the barn cutaway to find, each rewarding a small thing. This follows your exploration achievement taste.
Add a farm dog companion that never speaks but shows feelings by how it stands. This follows your wordless-companion idea.
Add county fair ribbons you collect by meeting fixed criteria with your animals and products. This follows your collecting habit.
Add old machinery restoration where you sort parts to bring an old tractor back, with a quiet log from its last owner. This follows your restoring-machines idea.
Add night rounds in the dark pasture where you spot what is off and file it in a catalogue. This follows your anomaly and eerie taste.
Add a lineage tree showing how your animals descend across generations. This follows your collecting and shelf-style progress taste.

Draw the farm as a pasture you can click: hover a paddock to see herd size, methane and income, and click to apply a lever such as feed change or capture. The levers sit on the farm instead of in a list.
Show a hover card on each gauge with its last five rounds and what moved it most. You see cause and effect without opening the report.
Add a right-click menu on a lever with Buy, Pin as a goal, Show cost over time and Compare with baseline farm. You get tools at your cursor.
Hold I to label every part of the pasture with what it is and which lever affects it. New players learn the farm by pointing.
Add a baseline-farm ghost mode where a second, greyed pasture beside yours shows the "grow unchecked" farm round by round with a drag handle between them. You see the decoupling payoff directly.
Let you resize the Report Card and dock it beside the pasture. You read your score while choosing levers.
Add a three-round lever planner where you queue levers for the next rounds and see a projected methane line before you commit. You can plan ahead like a strategy game.
Show the Collection and lever history as a sortable table with a click that replays that round's state. You can browse your farm's story like a save file.
Add a big-screen live graph of herd, methane and funds that fills the lower centre on wide monitors. Trends are always visible.
Add a UI scale slider and a high-contrast outline mode in Settings. The game stays readable on any monitor.
Make the farm a portrait scene with levers as large cards below it, where a swipe on a card buys it and a long-press shows the cost over time. A round plays with one thumb.
Pin round, funds and methane in a thin sticky top strip that gently changes label when methane crosses a band. The main trade-off stays in sight.
Put levers in a sideways shelf of large tiles above Advance, grouped as feed, herd and capture. You pick a lever without scrolling the page.
Show methane as a tall thermometer on the screen edge that opens its breakdown sheet when tapped. The key risk stays in view.
Make the baseline-farm comparison a flip card where a tap turns your farm into the unchecked-growth farm. You compare with one tap.
Let a pull-down on the farm advance one round with a confirm tick. A one-gesture turn suits tired thumbs.
Add a calm barn mode that dims the pasture, slows the animals, and shows only a single "healthy farm" word and the advance button. It suits bed-time play.
Add a herd-size slider with a big handle and live methane and income numbers above it. A herd decision feels direct.
Show the Report Card as a swipeable stack of cards (score, methane, funds, herd), one per screen. A report fits a phone.
Add an undo bar for the last lever bought, kept until you advance. A mis-tap costs nothing.
Add settlement voices: a village on thawing ground, a mining company and a scientist each ask for something different, and you weigh their views. You see the human side from several viewpoints.
Add foundation upgrades for roads and buildings on thawing ground. You learn adaptation as well as slowing the thaw.
Add linked tipping: when one region tips, the others tip slightly earlier. You see how tipping points can cascade.
Add a two-line chart splitting methane (strong, short) from carbon dioxide (weaker, long). You learn why the two gases act differently.
Add thaw lakes that appear on the map when ground collapses. You get a visual, real feature of thawing permafrost.
Add region profiles (Siberian yedoma, Alaskan boreal, Canadian peat) with carbon density and key facts read live from a named source. Each region feels like a real place.
Add a live feedback loop diagram that lights up as you advance a round. You can see cause and effect, not just read about it.
Add world-at-plus-degrees scene previews that show the land at +1, +2 and +3 degrees. You see what a number actually means.
Add a summit every ten rounds where all three regions pool a bonus if each stays under a threshold. You learn cooperation pays.
Add a background pathway picker (low, middle, high) labelled with published scenario names read live from a named source. You choose the future you are playing against.
Add core sample views: monitoring a region reveals layers of frozen ground, each with a short note. You get a satisfying reveal of what is hidden below.
Add shrub spread as a counterpoint: greening can darken the land and warm it further. You see that feedbacks can cut both ways.
Add calendar year labels on the graphs alongside round numbers. You can see how the story maps onto real time.
Let you pick Region B or C as your main region, each with its own starting conditions and lessons. You get new playthroughs without a new game.
Add a late-start rescue scenario that begins at +2.5 degrees with two regions already tipped. You get a hopeful challenge about limiting damage, not just preventing it.
Add an animals panel (caribou, Arctic fox, snow geese) showing how their ranges shrink with warming, with status read live from a named source such as the IUCN. You see who else is affected.
Add an albedo bar showing how much of the map is bright snow versus dark ground as it changes. You see another feedback at work.
Add an active layer depth gauge showing how deep the summer thaw reaches each round. You get the key permafrost measurement in one clear number.
Add funding source choices (grants, taxes, private investors), each with different strings attached. You see where climate money really comes from.
Add decade themes (wet, dry, fire-prone) that are announced in advance and change thaw rates in fixed ways. You get replay variety you can plan for.
Add tipping point cards: each time a region tips, a card records the round, the temperature and what you did before. You get a record of each story, even the hard ones.
Add a fewer-numbers mode showing arrows and words (warming fast, steady, slowing) instead of decimals. The game becomes easier to read for people who find numbers heavy.
Add a land-use dial for each region (tourism, mining, grazing, conservation) with different income and thaw effects. You get a richer way to balance funds against risk.
Add peatland rewetting as a new action that restores wet ground to hold carbon. You get a hopeful, real way to act beyond preserve and monitor.
Show the hottest region's status in the browser tab title. You can tell how the world is doing from another tab.
Add a drone fleet: you build, name and upgrade low-poly monitoring drones, and each upgrade is a small wiring puzzle. This brings robots and logic puzzles into the game.
Add field team missions: send a small team to help a failing research station or a village with sinking ground, with no clock and a retry if it goes wrong. It gives you a helper role.
Add the station AI's log, written in the quiet voice of a gentle program that is slowly breaking and remembers one mistake it made. You get a tragic, quiet character who comments on your run.
Add an Ice Core Archive of thirty cores, each from a different era with a short fact read live from a named source such as NOAA's paleoclimate data. You get a collection to complete.
Add a Long Winter watch mode: the station runs your saved plan slowly while a one-line log scrolls past, for leaving on a second screen. It is a calm mode with a friendly summary when you return.
Add polar whiteout, where distant regions are hidden in fog until sensor towers reveal them. This follows your foggy, dark and exploration taste.
Add two stations, one ice sheet: two friends run alternate regions and share monitoring data by invite link. This follows your optional friend ties and co-op taste.
Add anomaly reports of odd permafrost readings (gas pockets, humming ground) that you investigate with three instruments. This follows your eerie anomaly and deduction taste.
Add a Mars polar station scenario where protecting subsurface ice matters for a colony. This follows your space and science-fiction taste.
Add a herder's crossing, where you help a reindeer herd find a safe route across thinning ground, shown from the herders' view. This follows your helper role and the multiple-viewpoints rule.
Add a phase-change bench where you heat and cool a block of ice to see heat flow. This follows your physics interest.
Add a sensor filter puzzle where you pick rules that strip noise from readings and reveal the real trend. This follows your coding and AI interest.
Add thaw finds, where melting exposes old objects (tusks, tools) that go on a shelf with sourced notes. This follows your history studies and collecting habit.
Add a hand-drawn field sketchbook whose pictures change as the land does. This follows your occasional liking for hand-drawn art.
Add satellite tasking, a scheduling puzzle choosing which passes watch which region, improving monitoring accuracy. This follows your space and computers taste.
Add a low-poly 3D tundra you can orbit, with melt lakes forming. This follows your low-poly look.
Add an instrument catalogue where you pick parts from a handed list to build monitoring stations and record 25 setups. This follows your parts-catalogue and loadout taste.
Add a station wake-up sequence where the station AI reboots and quietly recaps while you were away. This follows your wish for a friendly welcome back.
Add a warm room, a low-poly stove-lit cabin you can rest in between rounds with a calm view. This follows your calm modes and dark-and-moody contrast.
Add a forecaster rank, where you guess next round's temperature before advancing and score how close you are. This follows your maths taste, and the guess visibly counts.
Add an ice road puzzle where you lay winter routes before they melt on a spatial map. This follows your spatial puzzle taste.
Add aurora photography, where you frame shots for an album. This follows your collecting and dark-sky taste.
Add an ice cave you explore by choosing paths with a lamp, with a map that fills in. This follows your exploration and creepy-place taste.
Add polar seasons that change the look: orange tundra in autumn, snow in winter. This follows your dream game's season changes.
Add test chambers, short rooms where you route heat with insulation and pumps to keep a sample frozen, with the station AI's dry commentary. This follows your Portal 2 favourite and puzzle taste.
Add an orphaned fox kit you care for, whose range and mood follow the health of your regions. This follows your caretaker role.
Add a sled packing puzzle before each field mission, where a good fit gives a bonus. This follows your liking for calm packing and tidy-up games.
Add a carbon flow picture, an animated diagram of where the carbon went. This follows your preference for pictures over charts.
Add secret terminal commands in the station console that unlock silly cosmetics. This follows your computers taste and cryptic hidden-achievement taste.
Add a pen-pal scientist at a distant station who sends postcards and small gifts as you progress. This follows your friendship and gifts taste.
Show the four regions as four panes with one shared time cursor, so dragging on one temperature graph moves the cursor on all four. You compare the same round across regions at a glance.
Add pattern markers and a clickable legend on the temperature chart to hide or show each region's line. You declutter the chart in one click.
Add a right-click menu on a region with Focus (hide the others), Pin to the side column and Show its science log. You can give one region the whole screen.
Let you click a funding amount and type a number, with the arrow keys for fine steps and Shift for big steps. Setting a split is quick on a keyboard.
Show the Carbon Bank as a wide table with sortable columns for deposit, round and dampening effect, plus a total row. You can read the lever like a ledger.
Add mouse-wheel zoom on the temperature graph to switch between the last 10 rounds and the whole run. You choose how close to look.
Add a Data window that lists every round's raw numbers in a table with a Copy as CSV button. You get a mod-style data viewer for your own analysis.
Add named window layouts such as "Forecasting" and "Review" that switch with F1 and F2. Each sitting gets the screen it needs.
Double-click a point on a graph to open that round's full details in a window. You inspect any past moment.
Add a science-log window with filters for region and event type and a search box. You find a specific warming event fast.
Add a bottom tab bar with A, B, C and D for the four regions, and let you swipe sideways between them. You can check any region with one thumb.
Replace funding sliders with a bar you drag, plus large plus and minus steps beside it. Splitting money is easy on a small screen.
Let you swipe a science log card away to mark it read, with the unread count shown on the tab. The log becomes a quick inbox you clear.
Add an escalating haptic pattern as temperature crosses each threshold, where the browser allows. The warming trend is something you feel.
Turn the phone sideways to show the four regions as a 2 by 2 grid of mini graphs. Landscape becomes a comparison board.
Let you pinch two region graphs together to overlay them on one chart, with the gap shaded. Comparing regions works with a gesture.
Add a one-region focus mode that shows only your region and shrinks the others to dots you can tap. The screen is calm and simple.
Let you read The Real Story as swipeable cards that work fully offline. A class break is enough to read one.
Add a Skip ahead three rounds button with a single summary screen at the end, using the same choices as before. A short session covers more ground.
Pull down on the main screen to open the climate archive as a bottom sheet. History is one gesture away.

Chain autopsy: after a chain closes, one panel points at the single cycle where you left the most savings on the table and shows the cheapest buy that would have fixed it. You get a clear "do this next time" lesson for your next chain.
Closing replay: when a chain closes, a short slow-motion replay redraws the whole ring filling up cycle by cycle. You get a satisfying victory scene to watch or skip.

Supplier choice: every few cycles you pick between two suppliers, one cheaper but dirtier and one dearer but cleaner, with both effects shown before you commit. You get a small real trade-off to weigh without any luck involved.

Second-hand market: instead of keeping a recovered unit in the loop you can sell it on to a second-hand market for funds at a lower price than new. You get a second way to earn money, and a tension between cash now and a tighter loop.

Material quality: every recycling pass slightly lowers a unit's quality, while repair and reuse keep it, and a quality bar shows the average. You get a reason to prefer repair over endless recycling, as in real life.

A fourth lever called Reduce: spend to make the product lighter so the same output needs fewer units, which cuts extraction without raising the circular share. You get a second route to winning to compare against closing the loop.

Busy and quiet seasons: demand rises and falls on a visible repeating rhythm, and a warehouse lets you store spare recovered material to cover the busy cycles. You get something to plan around that is fully predictable.
Focus view: tap any ring node and everything unrelated dims so you can follow just that node's flows in and out. You get a much easier read of a busy chain.

Partner favours: trade partners you deal with steadily grow friendlier and offer slightly better rates, shown as a small trust bar per partner. You get a reason to stick with a partner instead of hopping between them.

Sorting bench: an optional little puzzle where you sort a pile of broken items into repair, reuse and recycle bins, and each good sort adds a small boost to that lever next cycle. You get a hands-on break from menu clicking that visibly helps the chain.

Workshop floor view: a small top-down scene of your workshop that gains a visible machine for each lever you buy, with items moving between them. You get a picture of your chain that feels like a place.

Certification ladder: keep a clean streak of low extraction for a set number of cycles to earn Bronze, Silver and Gold chain certificates that give a small permanent price bonus on that chain. You get steady mini-goals between the big milestones.
Pilot programme: pay a small fee to trial a lever for three cycles at reduced strength before committing to the full price. You get a safe way to test a strategy and still learn from it.

Half-time score line: during a chain a small line says "if the chain ended now your score would be this, and this is what moves it most". You get a clear sense of how you are doing before the end screen.

A food and packaging goods category with its own levers, such as returnable crates and composting, where spoilage adds a new pressure. You get a fifth chain that plays differently from clothing, phones and furniture.
Category comparison table: a plain table showing why each goods category is harder or easier to loop, such as how long it lasts and how repairable it is. You get a clear reason to try each one.
Payback badges: each lever shows "pays back in about N cycles" at the current prices. You get a quick way to compare purchases without doing sums.
Growing demand mode: the production target rises by a set step every ten cycles, so a loop you have closed must keep growing to stay closed. You get a long game with a steady, predictable climb.

Finite mine scenario: the raw material source shrinks every cycle in a visible way, so extraction gets dearer the longer you rely on it. You get a scenario where the loop is not just good but necessary.
Island mode: a clearly labelled variant with trade switched off, with its own records. You get a pure self-reliance challenge to compare with normal play.
Branching toolbox: start with one lever, and every five cycles pick one of two new levers to unlock. You get chains that feel different each time you play, with no luck involved.
Source chart: a stacked chart of where each cycle's supply came from, split into new, repaired, reused and recycled. You get a picture that shows your strategy at a glance.
Product toy: a small playground where you slide how often one product is repaired and see how long it lasts and how much it saves. You get to feel the idea before you spend anything.

Temptation mode: from cycle one you are already circular, and each cycle a cheap extraction deal is offered that you can accept or refuse, with its cost to the loop shown. You get a chance to see what slipping would cost.
Company name and motto: name your firm and write a short motto that appears on the end screen and the copied result. You get a bit of ownership over your chain.

Robot crew: robots staff your repair, reuse and recycling stations, and each is a collectible with a quirk you can level to 5 to unlock a station perk. You get the "raise this to 5 to unlock that" goals you like, in a robot-and-workshop frame.
Scrap station start: an alternate scenario set on a dark orbital scrap station, with the same rules but a space look. You get Loop in your favourite setting.

Strategy catalogue: the game recognises named strategies, such as repair-first or trade-heavy, and lists each one you have closed a chain with, with a completion count. You get a collector's list that rewards trying different builds.
Pick-up note: when you come back, a friendly line tells you where you stopped and the one cheapest step to the next milestone. You get a warm welcome back with an easy first move.
Circular City: short 8-cycle missions that each add a district to a growing city map when you finish them. You get short wins that build into a bigger picture.

Supply Lines messages: a worker at a struggling factory texts you each cycle and you answer from a few replies, with branching paths and an optional skip. You get a short story told through your chain (your Lifeline taste).

Sorting droid: a small silent droid at the bench shows pride, worry or relief with a few simple faces after each cycle. You get a quiet robot companion who shows feeling without speaking (your droid taste).
Auditor's footnotes: dry, dark one-line notes from a bored auditor under the ledger, kept clear of any harmful jokes. You get humour in the tone you like (your dry-and-dark taste).
Tonnage counter: a lifetime counter of material saved that rolls from kilograms to tonnes to kilotonnes as you play. You get numbers that keep growing huge (your big-number taste).
Secret synergies: two far-apart patents combine into a surprisingly strong effect, hinted only by a cryptic line. You get the thrill of finding the one broken combo (your broken-build taste).
Two-halves chain: you run extraction to factory, a friend runs use to disposal, and you pass units by a short code. You get a co-op puzzle that needs real teamwork (your Keep Talking taste).
Kind notes: leave a friend's finished chain one note chosen from ten friendly preset lines. You get a friend tie with no chat (your gifts-and-notes taste).
Overnight tidy: when you return, a small stock of sorted units is waiting, with a capped, friendly summary. You get a welcome back that gives you something (your idle-reward taste).
Recovery plan: when damage spikes, a card lists three steps to restore the chain, each one reachable. You get a "kind of failed, here is how to fix it" path (your restore-progress taste).
Product sticker book: one sticker for every product whose full life you have followed, with a percentage bar. You get a one-of-everything collection (your collect-everything taste).
Riddle achievements: a set of achievements whose descriptions are cryptic riddles rather than a question mark. You get hidden goals that still give a clue (your cryptic-description taste).
Mass balance bench: a puzzle where inputs must equal outputs plus waste in grams, and solving it improves a lever. You get a small chemistry-style puzzle that helps your chain (your chemistry taste).

Pipe routing boards: connect each recycling output to the right factory input with paths that cannot cross, Flow Free style. You get a puzzle you already love, paying a bonus to the chain (your Flow Free taste).
Rule bender: slide word tiles such as "repair costs less" to rewrite a chain rule in a small sandbox. You get a Baba Is You style puzzle in Loop's world (your rule-puzzle taste).
Tidy shelf: unpack a crate of recovered items onto a workshop shelf where each has a natural home. You get a calm, Unpacking-like moment between cycles (your Unpacking taste).
Expert chain viewer: watch a recorded strong chain at your own pace with the reasons shown beside each move. You get the walkthrough you would look up, built in (your watch-a-100%-run taste).
Micro-trophies: a tiny trophy pops up for each small first, such as your first repair of a new product. You get a reward every minute or so (your small-rewards taste).
Ration city: a walled, dark city-state scenario with strict quotas where the loop must close inside the walls. You get a dystopian setting with a clear goal (your dystopia taste).
Generation ship: a long-haul ship that can import nothing, so every material must close. You get a space version with the hardest loop (your space taste).
Rule blocks: build a three-line standing plan from drop-down blocks, such as "if damage is over 60 then repair", that runs each cycle. You get a gentle first taste of coding (your coding taste).
Three viewpoints: each shock is described by an owner, a repair worker and a shopper, who each judge it differently. You get to compare points of view (your multiple-viewpoints taste).
Fast ramp: only one lever at the start, and the rest unlock within the first eight cycles. You get an opening that is simple and then speeds up quickly (your easy-start-then-ramp taste).
Unfolding workshop: new rooms and options appear as one line each in a log as you progress, like A Dark Room. You get discovery without a tutorial (your A Dark Room taste).
Full completion bar: one percentage bar covering the categories, name plates, strategies and certificates. You get a clear, reachable 100 percent (your reachable-100% taste).
Huge patent tree: grow the patent tree into dozens of nodes in long branches per lever, with no refunds. You get the big tree you asked for (your huge-skill-tree taste).
Let you drag a handle on each ring node to set how much goes to repair, reuse and recycle, with the flow lines redrawing as you drag. You shape the loop by hand and watch it change.
Let Shift plus 1, 2 or 3 apply a saved spending split to the round. You can run a favourite plan with one chord.
Add mouse-wheel zoom and drag pan on the trade network. Large networks stay readable on a monitor.
Add a right-click menu on a goods category with Relabel, Pin, Show its chain and Compare with last cycle. Common jobs sit at your cursor.
Add a split view with the chain diagram on the left, a table of materials per cycle on the right and a draggable divider. You see the picture and the numbers together.
Add Ctrl+Z and Ctrl+Y across a cycle's investment changes with a small history list you can click. You can try ideas and step back freely.
Hold Alt over a ring node to show a ghost of what would change if you added one more unit of spending. You preview a choice without making it.
Add a pinned goal bar with three circular-share markers you set yourself (for example 40, 60 and 80 percent). Your three goals are always visible.
Save the layout of your open windows as "Planning" or "Review" and switch with F1 and F2. The screen fits the sitting.
Let a middle-click on a node invest one step and a Shift-click invest ten. Mouse players get fast bulk changes.
Let you tap a ring node to open a bottom sheet where you drag one slider to split spending. The loop can be redesigned with a thumb.
Keep the Advance Cycle button as a wide bar at the bottom with a thin ring around it showing the circular share. The main action and goal share one control.
Show the circular percent as a large number that changes colour band with a pattern as well, pinned at the top. The main goal is always visible.
Let a swipe on the ring show last cycle's ring beside this one. Progress appears as a before and after.
Swipe a goods card left to relabel it. A common job becomes a gesture.
Add a large-print mode that enlarges node labels and flow numbers while keeping the diagram on one screen. The ring stays readable for tired eyes.
Turn the phone sideways to show the loop diagram on the left and the investments on the right. Landscape becomes a workshop view.
Double-tap the diagram to fit it to the screen and pinch to zoom into a node. The ring stays legible on small phones.
Let a long-press on a node show a plain-words card of what flows in and out. Detail comes without a hover.
Add a half-asleep one-button mode that applies your last split and advances. A tired player still moves the loop forward.

Arrival mix: newcomers arrive as a mix of families, single adults, older people and children with different needs, shown as a small composition bar each round. You get a reason to match services to who actually arrived instead of one headcount.

Voices panel: after each round four short comments appear from newcomers, long-time residents, local business owners and city staff, each reacting from their own point of view. You get to see that the same decision lands differently for different people.

Community partners: local groups such as a school board, a faith hall or a workers' club offer help for a favour in return, and you choose which to sign up. You get new allies to build around, each with its own price.

Who is left behind: the end-of-run screen shows wellbeing split by group rather than one average, and names the group that did worst. You get an honest picture of whether the region worked for everyone.

Modular versus permanent housing: fast, cheap modular units help right away but cost more to run each round, while permanent homes are slow and dear but cheap to keep. You get a classic build-now-or-build-well choice.
Arrival shapes: choose a starting pattern of arrivals such as a sudden surge, a slow trickle or two waves, each with a plain-words description. You get very different early games without any luck.

Festival planning: a cohesion festival now and then lets you pick one theme, such as food, sport or craft, each helping a different part of the community. You get a friendly, low-stress decision between the big spending rounds.
Opportunity line: after you spend, a small line says what that same money could have bought instead, in plain words. You get a clearer feel for the real cost of each choice.

Volunteer hours: a second resource that grows from cohesion and is spent on things money cannot buy, such as buddy programmes and language cafes. You get a second budget to juggle that rewards good community-building.

Policy lens: switch a round's summary between three viewpoints, market-led, state-led and community-led, to see how each would describe your costs and results. You get to compare approaches without being told which is right.

Pathway view: a visible funnel showing how many newcomer households are at each step, such as shelter, registration, language, school and work, with the clogged step highlighted. You get a clear picture of exactly where your system is stuck.

Local election beat: every 20 rounds an election is held, and the result follows from how cohesive the region is, changing which policies are cheaper for the next stretch. You get a long-arc consequence for how you treated the community, with no randomness.
Quick primer: a 30-second hands-on demo of strain and capacity before your first round, where you drag a slider and watch what happens. You get the key idea without reading a manual.
Why-did-it-change hover: tap a gauge to see the top three things that moved it last round. You get cause and effect made visible.
Skills pool: arrivals bring skills, such as nursing, building and teaching, and you can place them into services for free capacity. You get newcomers as a resource and not only a cost.
Language ladder: language classes move newcomers up visible levels, and each level opens more jobs. You get a clear long-term pathway to build.
Score explainer: a page showing exactly how wellbeing is worked out, with sliders to try different values. You get a full understanding of what the game is measuring.
Reserve fund: set aside part of your income into a savings pot that softens budget cuts later. You get a way to plan ahead for tough rounds.
Rescue puzzles: hand-made snapshots of a region mid-crisis, such as round 40 with high strain, where you try to stabilise it in ten rounds. You get short focused challenges beyond the full run.
Rent dial: a policy slider that sets how housing is priced, shown with its different effects on newcomers, long-time residents and landlords. You get a hard trade-off with several viewpoints in it.

Neighbour book: every household you house becomes a card in a book with a short invented note, and you fill the pages for each background. You get a collector's goal inside a game where you are the helper.
Three goals panel: Drift shows three goals at all times with no order, such as "services to 60", "five perfect fits" and "reach Stable". You get the goal layout you like best.
Night watch: a dim, calm screen for the autopilot that shows the region's windows lighting up as it runs. You get a relaxed way to leave it on late at night.
Arkship mode: the same game retold as a space habitat taking in refugees from a failing colony, with ring-ships in place of towns. You get your space setting for the same systems.
Region charter: every five-round council goal you clear adds a clause to a charter page that grows as you play. You get short wins that build into a document you can read.
Sister region: paste a friend's finished-run code and their region appears on your map as a sister, giving a small shared bonus to both. You get an optional friend tie with no chat.

Caseworker messages: a caseworker texts you about one family across the run and you answer from a few replies, with branching paths and an optional skip. You get a Lifeline-style story as the helper (your Lifeline taste).
Survey drone: a silent little drone follows new arrivals and shows simple emotes such as relief or worry. You get a quiet robot companion (your droid taste).
Welcome desk puzzle: match arriving families to open homes by size and needs in a small packing puzzle that feeds integration. You get a hands-on helper puzzle (your helper and spatial-puzzle taste).
Road routing boards: connect homes to schools and clinics with paths that cannot cross, Flow Free style. You get a favourite puzzle with a visible reward (your Flow Free taste).
Region cookbook: recipes are handed to you when a household settles, and serving one at a festival gives a bonus. You get handed recipes and a collection (your handed-recipes taste).
Civic shelf: a model of each building type, such as clinic, school and library, appears on a shelf once built, with a percentage bar. You get a one-of-each collection (your collect-everything taste).
Twin councils: two friends each run half of one region, housing and services, passing a short code each round. You get a co-op puzzle (your Keep Talking taste).
Welcome basket: leave a friend's region a welcome basket that shows as a flag in their log. You get a friend gift with no chat (your gifts-and-notes taste).
Climb-back list: when the region slips a band, a short list of three steps shows how to restore it. You get a way back instead of a fail (your restore-progress taste).
Records terminal: a dark console where you filter households by simple rules, such as waiting four rounds or more. You get a bit of database thinking as a tool (your coding taste).
Ratio puzzle: at each council milestone a quick sum, such as classrooms for 120 children at 25 each, earns a discount. You get a maths puzzle that matters (your maths taste).
Fog of need: an optional hard mode where each group's needs are hidden until the group arrives. You get a harder choice you opt into (your hard-mode-as-option taste).
People welcomed counter: a lifetime counter that climbs into the thousands with a small celebration at each milestone. You get numbers that grow big (your big-number taste).
Huge civic tree: policies grow into a large branching tree of housing, health, learning, trade and safety, with no refunds. You get a big tree (your huge-skill-tree taste).
Round ticks: each round ends with a short cheerful list such as "3 families housed, 1 child started school". You get small rewards every minute (your small-rewards taste).
Letter from a resident: when you return, a short letter from a resident mentions where you left off. You get a friendly welcome back (your welcome-back taste).
Move-in scenes: a calm scene where a household's rooms are unpacked item by item as they settle. You get a quiet, Unpacking-like moment (your Unpacking taste).

Closed-doors what-if: a darker alternate run where the region shuts its doors, shown beside your real run. You get a dystopian contrast with several viewpoints (your dystopia and multiple-viewpoints taste).
Basics board: food, water, health and shelter shown as four simple meters for every group. You get the basic needs you care about in one view (your human-rights taste).
Safe-house service: a service for people who need to be safe, with its own need curve and plain explanation. You get a way to help people you care about (your women's-and-personal-rights taste).
Repeat last plan: one big button reuses last round's choices so you can play half asleep. You get a calm routine you know by heart (your routine taste).
Schematic view: the region drawn as a dark blueprint with glowing lines. You get a computer-board look (your Tron and computers taste).
Wellbeing weather: wellbeing shown as sky and weather over the region as well as numbers. You get pictures instead of charts (your pictures-over-numbers taste).
Strain lab: a toy with sliders showing how capacity and strain move together. You get a physics-style playground (your maths and physics taste).
Make the district view pannable and zoomable with the mouse wheel and a drag, with a click on a building showing who lives there and its strain. The region becomes a place you explore.
Show a hover card on each gauge (capacity, strain, integration, wellbeing, pending) with the last five rounds and the biggest change. You see why a number moved.
Add a right-click menu on a building with Invest, Show people housed and Compare with neighbour. Common jobs sit at the cursor.
Let you resize and tile the Round Ledger, Region Collection and Long-Horizon Outcomes windows side by side, remembering the arrangement. You can study the long story across three views.
Add Ctrl+F on the district map that highlights buildings by name or type. You find a building without scanning the map.
Keep a sticky bar with the current band, strain and a mini trend line that stays put as you pan the map. Your key numbers never leave the screen.
Add Tab order and focus rings through the district's buildings, with Enter to open one. You can browse the region without a mouse.
Add a mouse-wheel timeline strip along the bottom where scrolling steps back through rounds and shows the district as it was. You can see the region change over time.
Hold Shift while hovering a building to compare it with the neighbouring region's matching building. You see what the other side has.
Add a Data window with every round's numbers in a sortable table and a Copy as CSV button. You can inspect your region like a modder.
Make the region visual a portrait map where a tap on a building opens a bottom sheet with Invest and details. Managing the district is a direct touch.
Let you swipe between your region and the neighbouring district as two full-screen cards. Comparing neighbours is a flick.
Keep Advance Round as a large bottom button with a small strain ring around it. The key action and key risk share one control.
Make long investment lists into collapsible groups with a sticky header showing the group's total cost. You skim a region's options in one screen.
Let a swipe on a gauge cycle between its value, its last ten rounds as a mini graph and a plain explanation. Each gauge becomes a three-sided card.
Add a text size picker (small, normal, large) with a live preview, remembered on the phone. Long labels stay comfortable to read.
Turn long lists of investments into cards you swipe right to buy. Choices are gestures.
Keep a sticky bar with the number of people arriving next round and an arrow for the trend. You always see what is coming while you scroll.
Let a long-press on any term open a bottom-sheet glossary line with a link to The Real Story. Definitions fit a small screen.
Add a quiet dusk mode that dims the region and hides all numbers except a single word for how the region feels. It suits bed-time play.

Colony megaprojects: a colony can be given a landmark, such as a space elevator or an orbital garden, that needs several different goods delivered over time and then shows on the map for good. You get a long-term, many-goods goal that makes your network visibly yours.
Triangle routes: one ship runs a loop through three colonies, dropping and picking up at each stop. You get a deeper routing puzzle than back-and-forth runs.
Named ships and logbooks: give each ship a name, and it keeps a logbook of its biggest hauls and longest voyages. You get a bit of attachment to your fleet.
Convoy bonus: ships on the same route that leave together share costs and arrive a little faster. You get a reason to time departures rather than send ships one by one.
Quarterly report: every so often a one-screen summary shows your best route, your worst, the biggest price swing and the colony that grew most. You get a tidy overview without opening five panels.
Ship liveries: paint schemes for your ships, chosen from a swatch list and unlocked by milestones. You get a cosmetic reward that shows up on the map.
Lane upgrades: spend credits to permanently shorten one route, shown as a thicker, brighter line on the map. You get a new way to invest and a map that grows richer.
Opportunity board: a short ranked list of the biggest surpluses nobody is collecting right now, with an estimated profit for each. You get an instant answer to "where should I send the next ship".
Network time-lapse: a button replays how your trade network grew from the first route to today. You get a pretty summary and a screenshot-worthy moment.
Price alerts: set a target price on a good and a marker appears on the map when the market reaches it, with no sound and no popup. You get to leave the game running and still catch the right moment.

Passenger liners: a second cargo type of people, valued for comfort and speed rather than price, which helps the destination colony develop faster. You get a different kind of route to run alongside goods.

Good finder: tap any good anywhere in the game to see where it is cheapest, where it is wanted most and the best known route between the two. You get a shortcut for planning that needs no spreadsheet.
Map filters: switch the map to show only one good's flow, where profit is highest, or which lanes have idle capacity. You get a clearer map when the network is big.
Gentle markets: an optional setting where prices never fall below a floor, for a relaxed start. You get a softer way in that you can switch off later.
Crash explainer: when a price crashes, a note says why in plain words, such as "you sold 40 units into a market that wanted 15". You get to learn from each swing.
Colony growth looks: colonies change their appearance on the map at each development level. You get visible proof of your work.
Starter loan: borrow credits early for a bigger ship, repaid out of a share of profit with no penalty for being slow. You get a way to speed up the opening without risk.
Quick restart after renewal: one tap rebuilds your two best routes from the last charter at starting prices. You get to skip the repeated opening.

Derelict network: a scenario where you inherit an old, abandoned company's network of colonies, ships and routes in poor shape and bring it back to life. You get a different opening to the usual one-ship start.
Fleet groups: put ships into named groups and give a whole group one order, such as change route or take a break. You get an easier way to manage a large fleet.
Colony wishlists: each colony shows three things it wants, and filling all three unlocks a gift at level 5. You get the "get X to level 5 to unlock Z" goals you like.
Relief runs: when a colony is short of something, you can send a free relief run for a permanent goodwill bonus and a thank-you note. You get a helper role in a trading game.
Colony postcards: each colony you develop sends a short invented postcard, and you collect the full album. You get a collector's goal with a gentle story.
Night freight: a calm view that follows one ship at a time across a dim map, with nothing needing a click. You get a quiet way to leave it running half asleep.
Ship minds: each automated ship gets a robot mind with a name and a quirk, and you collect all of them. You get a robots-and-collecting hook inside the trading loop.
Low-poly galaxy view: an optional rotating low-poly view of the colonies and lanes, dark and moody. You get your favourite look on top of the same game.
Stranded captain: a freighter captain texts you for trade advice over branching days, with an optional skip. You get a Lifeline-style story inside the game (your Lifeline taste).

The failing hauler: an old auto-hauler whose logs are corrupting, and delivering certain goods restores its memories one by one. You get a quiet, tragic machine character to repair (your Rinzler taste).
Port bulletins: dry, dark one-line notices from the port authority, kept clear of harmful jokes. You get humour in your tone (your dry-and-dark taste).
Cargo shelf: a low-poly crate for each good you have shipped, with a percentage bar. You get a one-of-each collection (your collect-everything taste).
Hull museum: a model of each hull you design, one per type, on a display shelf. You get a design record (your character-designer taste).
Joint venture: two friends each run one cluster and pass goods across by short codes. You get a co-op puzzle (your Keep Talking taste).
Guest trader: a friend's best colony appears as a visiting trader on your map. You get an optional friend tie with no chat (your friends-help-each-other taste).
Tow home: a ship that gets into trouble is towed to the dock and repaired by delivering parts. You get a restore-instead-of-fail path (your restore-progress taste).

Planet alignment windows: some lanes are faster when colonies line up on their orbits, shown on a wheel that you can predict. You get a physics-flavoured planning puzzle (your physics and predictability taste).
Logic dispatch board: wire AND and OR chips that trigger automatic dispatches. You get a mini circuit puzzle as automation (your logic-gates taste).
Delivered blueprints: colonies hand you recipes when they reach level 3. You get handed recipes (your handed-recipes taste).
Huge charter tree: grow the charter tree into dozens of nodes with no refunds. You get a big tree (your huge-skill-tree taste).
Credit names: very large credit totals get stylish names beyond billions. You get exponential growth that feels good (your big-number taste).
Wild builds: certain captain, hull and route combinations are very strong and hinted by cryptic lines. You get the thrill of finding the one broken build (your broken-build taste).
Welcome-back ledger: on return, a ledger lists what your automated fleet shipped, within a friendly cap. You get something for being away (your idle-reward taste).
Dock routine: an optional five-step checklist you do the same way each visit. You get a routine you know by heart (your routine taste).
Umbral Deep mood: the dark cluster gets its own dim, foggy look. You get a moody setting (your dark-and-moody taste).

Anomaly sightings: odd markers on lanes, such as a silent ship or a repeating beacon, filed in a field catalogue with nothing attacking you. You get a creepy, calm collection (your anomaly-game taste).
Rebuild missions: ten short missions that together tell the story of reopening a lost sector. You get short wins that build one story (your short-wins taste).
Basics bar: food, water and medicine per colony shown as one plain bar. You get the human needs you care about in view (your food-water-healthcare taste).
Dock disputes: when a colony and a rival firm want the same route, three viewpoints are shown and you choose with no right answer. You get several points of view (your multiple-viewpoints taste).
Ghost routes: on your first visit faint ghost routes show what to try, then disappear. You get no-tutorial learning (your work-it-out taste).
Cargo packing: a calm puzzle packing crates into a hold, which sets how efficiently a ship loads. You get a spatial puzzle with a payoff (your spatial-puzzle taste).
Needs-you strip: a quiet strip that only lights up when something requires a decision, so you can half-watch. You get a class-friendly way to play (your half-attention taste).
Make the map a full-window star chart with mouse-wheel zoom, drag pan and a click-and-drag to draw a new route from one colony to another. Building a trade network feels like a real strategy game.
Show a hover card on each colony with its needs, stockpile and the ships serving it. You read a colony without opening a window.
Add a right-click menu on a ship with Send to colony, Set priority, Rename and Show its history. Fleet orders sit at the cursor.
Let you drag ships from the Fleet Captains list onto routes on the map to assign them, with a preview of profit per trip. Assigning a fleet is direct and visual.
Add box-select on the map to pick several ships with a drag and give them a shared order. You can move a group in one action.
Add Ctrl+1 to Ctrl+9 control groups for ships and colonies, and 1 to 9 to jump to them. Experienced players get an RTS-style quick recall.
Add a route-profit overlay on key P that shades routes by profit with a pattern as well as colour. You spot weak routes at a glance.
Show a permanent ledger ribbon along the bottom of a wide monitor that scrolls profit per route in real time. Income is always in view.
Let Alt-click on a colony open its trade-post window and Shift-click add it to the route you are drawing. The mouse does more with modifier keys.
Add save slots as a file-style list with a map thumbnail, profit and automation slots for each. Loading is a proper PC menu.
Make the map a portrait view where you tap a colony and then another to draw a route, with a bottom sheet to assign a ship. Route building is a two-tap job.
Put ships in a horizontal strip above the thumb zone that you can tap to open their orders. Fleet control is one-handed.
Let a long-press on a ship open a radial menu with Send, Assign route and Rename. Fleet orders are one gesture.
Add a Send all idle ships button that gives each idle ship its last route and shows a summary sheet. A short session keeps the fleet working.
Add a home-screen card with profit per minute, automation slots used and the next colony need. You can check on the empire in class.
Let you pinch to zoom the map and double-tap a colony to centre it. The map works like a phone map.
Add a half-asleep mode that shows one big card for the most valuable idle ship with a Send button. A tired player can keep the network running with a tap.
Add a battery-saver mode that stops ship animation and updates positions every few seconds. The phone lasts longer.
Swipe a colony card left to see its needs and right to see its stockpile. A colony fits a card.
Turn the market table into cards sorted by profit with a long-press that opens a price history sheet. Trading data fits a phone.

Wonder of the age: each era offers one wonder that the whole settlement builds across many seasons from shared labour and materials, with its own model in the 3D scene. You get a big shared goal in every era.

Festival calendar: choose a few annual festivals for your settlement, each unlocked by research and each lifting a different livability area. You get a gentle choice that makes seasons feel different.

District focus: after a district has grown, pick what it specialises in, such as market, scholars or harbour, and its buildings change shape to match. You get a city whose neighbourhoods have real character.
Advance until something needs you: one button runs seasons forward and stops the moment a choice, an event or a shortage appears. You get a faster way through quiet stretches.
Research map: the whole research tree as one zoomable graph that shows what leads to what and what you can already reach. You get a clear picture of where you are headed.
Renovate in place: upgrade an old building into its new-era version instead of tearing it down and rebuilding. You get a cheaper, kinder way to modernise.

Puzzle scenarios: hand-made starts with one stated goal, for example feeding 200 people on an island with almost no farmland, each with a par number of seasons. You get short, focused challenges beyond the open run.
Caravans: trade with neighbours shows small caravans walking between settlements in the 3D scene. You get a visible sign that your trade is happening.
Era report card: at each era transition a one-page report grades food, safety, knowledge and livability, with one plain tip for the next era. You get a clear sense of how each era went.
Policy forecast: before adopting a policy, small arrows show what it is likely to do to each stat over the next few seasons. You get to choose with your eyes open.
Era primer card: the first time you enter an era a short card explains its new mechanic with a tiny worked example. You get a gentle start in each era.
Demographics: a panel showing children, workers and elders in your settlement and how each group affects food, labour and care. You get a deeper layer under the headcount.
Schools and literacy: schools and libraries raise a literacy rate that speeds up research. You get a clear cause for faster progress.
Health: a health stat that rises with clean water, clinics and good food and is shown with its causes. You get another thread to manage, with steady cause and effect and no random plagues.
Energy mix: in later eras you plan how your power is made, such as wood, coal, water, sun and nuclear, with cost and sustainability shown. You get a puzzle that connects to your livability score.
Harvest planner: a calendar view of which crops and labour fit which season so you can plan ahead. You get a tool that rewards forward thinking.
Look Back slider: drag a slider to morph a settlement's skyline between two eras. You get a fun way to see how far you have come.
Vision cards: when founding, choose a long-term vision, such as trading hub, seat of learning or garden city, which sets three themed goals. You get replay variety that is not random.
Guided tour: a button that flies the camera through your settlement stopping at each district with its story. You get a calm way to enjoy what you built.
Diet variety: a stat for how many different foods you grow, which helps health and resilience. You get a reason to diversify rather than farm one crop.
Lantern keeper: a hands-on mode where you walk the city carrying supplies to residents who need them, each delivery lifting a stat. You get a first-person helper role inside your city.
Relic hunt: each era leaves relics to find in the Look Back views, eight per era, filling a museum case. You get a collection with a clear 100 percent.
Night and fog look: a preset that shows the 3D city at night with lantern glow and low fog. You get the dark, moody feel you like.
Robot caretakers: in the last eras you commission and name robot helpers that each take a job, and collect all the models. You get your robots theme late in the game.
Era sprints: play one era alone from a fixed start in under 20 minutes, with a medal that fills a tile on a grid of all eight. You get short wins that add up to the full picture.

Radio from beyond: in the Relay Age a faint signal arrives and you answer a stranger over branching days, as a hobbyist with a radio. You get a Lifeline-style story (your Lifeline and radio-tinkerer taste).
Field guide: every crop, animal and material is logged on its first sighting, with a percentage bar. You get a one-of-each notebook (your collect-everything taste).
Recipe scrolls: crafting chains are handed to you when a building is researched. You get handed recipes (your handed-recipes taste).
Two-city alliance: two friends found settlements on one map, one covering food and the other tools, trading by code each season. You get a co-op puzzle (your Keep Talking taste).
Visitor stones: friends can leave a small cairn with a preset message on your archive card. You get a friend tie with no chat (your gifts-and-notes taste).
Rebuilding path: after a collapse, a guided path keeps survivors and part of your knowledge so you can restore the settlement. You get a way back, not a restart (your restore-progress taste).
City console: a dark console where you query the city, such as population by district. You get a computer-style tool (your computers taste).
Life-support boards: in the Space Age, balance oxygen, carbon dioxide and water on a board, and solved boards add habitat capacity. You get a chemistry-style puzzle (your chemistry taste).
Water network: wells, aqueducts and pumps drawn as lines with a coverage map. You get the basic need you care about (your water-access taste).
Basics overlay: a map view showing which districts lack food, water, shelter or care. You get a clear picture of who needs help (your helper taste).

Charter of rights: adopt rights across eras, each with costs, effects and the viewpoints of different groups. You get a history-and-rights game with several viewpoints (your history and human-rights taste).
Big-number notation: late-era population and knowledge scale into millions with tidy labels. You get growth that feels huge (your big-number taste).
Broken research combo: two far research branches combine into an outsized effect hinted by a cryptic line. You get the one broken combo to find (your broken-build taste).
Steward's stockpile: a steward leaves a small capped stockpile while you are away, with a friendly welcome. You get something for returning (your idle-reward taste).
The old machine: a Relay Age relay AI that once saved the city and now fades, whose memories you restore through research. You get a tragic, quiet character (your Rinzler taste).
Narrator: an optional dry narrator who comments on, and sometimes argues with, your choices. You get a Stanley Parable feel (your Stanley Parable taste).
Founding chapters: five-minute civic missions that together tell the story of the founding. You get short wins that build one story (your short-wins taste).
Rocket program: assemble launch stages from parts and tune ratios to reach orbit. You get a Kerbal-style puzzle (your space-and-physics taste).
Era mastery bars: a percentage bar per era covering achievements, buildings, research and citizens. You get a reachable 100 percent (your reachable-100% taste).
Scouting the fog: scouts clear fogged land and a map-completion percentage rises. You get exploration and completion (your fog and exploration taste).
Material board: a periodic-table style board that fills as new materials are unlocked. You get a chemistry collection (your chemistry and collecting taste).
Riddle achievements: a set of achievements with cryptic riddle descriptions. You get hidden goals that give a clue (your cryptic-description taste).
Expert settlement viewer: watch a strong settlement at your own pace with reasons beside each choice. You get the walkthrough built in (your watch-a-100%-run taste).
Picture stats: an option to show food, safety and knowledge as parts of the skyline rather than numbers. You get pictures over numbers (your pictures-over-numbers taste).
Fast first era: the Tribal era teaches by doing with two buildings and speeds up within a few seasons. You get an easy start that ramps quickly (your easy-start-then-ramp taste).
Add mouse-wheel zoom, middle-drag orbit and right-drag pan on the 3D settlement, with the 1 to 4 camera presets kept as shortcuts. The scene becomes a proper strategy-game view.
Show a hover card on every building in the 3D scene with its output, workers and the next upgrade. You read the settlement by pointing.
Add a right-click menu on a building with Upgrade, Assign workers, Show its research and Look back. Common jobs sit at the cursor.
Add a wide mission-control layout that tiles the City Views dashboard, the civic map and the flow diagram as three docked panes with resizable dividers. A big monitor holds the whole city.
Add WASD and edge-of-screen camera movement in the 3D scene with Q and E to rotate and Shift for speed. The camera moves like in a city builder.
Add a Ctrl+K command palette to jump to a research node, building, citizen, heritage site or era by name. You find things by typing.
Let the log sit as a docked, scrollable side panel with filter chips for events, research and citizens on a wide screen. History stays in view.
Add save slots as a file-style list with era, population and a small 3D snapshot of each settlement. Loading looks like a real PC game menu.
Add window layouts such as "Builder", "Council" and "Archive", switched with F1 to F3. Each sitting gets the screen it needs.
Add a mod-style Data window that lists every building, tech and citizen in sortable tables with a Copy button. You can study the game's numbers.
Make the 3D scene full-screen in portrait with a one-finger orbit, a pinch to zoom, and a bottom sheet that opens when you tap a building. The settlement is something you touch.
Keep the camera presets as four large buttons along the bottom edge, with a fifth for "my last view". Camera changes are one tap.
Add a bottom tab bar (City, Research, Look back, Log) so the main areas are one thumb tap apart. The big game fits four tabs.
Reset the camera to the last preset with a two-finger tap on the 3D scene. A lost camera is fixed in one gesture.
Add a first-run picker for text size and 3D detail (small, standard, large) that sets phone-friendly defaults. The game starts comfortable instead of cramped.
Add a low-power 2D view for old phones that replaces the 3D scene with a flat illustrated map and the same tap sheet. Weak phones still get a full game.
Add swipeable era cards in the Look Back panel with a tap to open each era's snapshot. History is a card flick.
Let a pull-down on the scene advance one season with a confirm tick. A one-gesture turn suits short sessions.
Add a half-asleep mode that dims the city, shows a single suggested action and a Next season button. A tired player can still make progress.
Add a settings option to cap the 3D frame rate and pixel density on phones. The game stays smooth and cool.

sections.title: Le Champ de Mots: general ideas

items.text: Dictation: hear a word or short phrase and type it with every accent. Correct answers water the matching plots, so it counts toward your practice score.

Say-the-right-thing scenes: short two-line exchanges in a shop, a station or a cafe where you pick the best reply from three, using the week's vocabulary. Each correct reply waters the plots for the words it used.

Pattern spotter: look at a group of verbs or nouns and work out the pattern yourself, such as which endings are feminine, before the rule is shown. The patterns you find are logged and count toward the practice score.

Word families: a small tree on each plot showing words built from the same root, such as jardin, jardinier and jardinage, with a quick question on each. Answers water the related plots, so one root teaches several words.
Drawn picture vocabulary: simple code-drawn icons for everyday nouns, so you can match picture to word. Every match waters its plot.
Study calendar: a calm heat calendar of the days you practised, with no streak counter and nothing taken away for a gap. You get a quiet picture of your progress.
Accent rules lesson: a short set of questions on when to use e acute, e grave, circumflex and cedilla, based on patterns in real words. Correct answers add to your practice score.

Short writing prompts: write two or three sentences on a topic, and the game checks that the required words and verb forms appear. You get writing practice with real feedback, and a visible writing count.
Journey map: your course as a winding road of villages, one per week, filling in as plots grow. You get an at-a-glance picture of how far you have come.
Your own vocabulary patch: add words from your class notes and they grow like any other plot with the same review rules. You get the game to cover exactly what you are studying.
Look-alike words: practise pairs people mix up, such as a and à, et and est, ou and où, or ses and ces. Each correct answer adds to a mix-up practice counter.
