Countries and cities: practise the small words for where you are going or coming from, such as en, au, aux and a. Correct answers water the grammar plots they match.
Numbers workshop: type spelled-out numbers, prices, dates and phone numbers, in both directions. Correct answers water the number plots and add to the practice score.
Time and dates: read a clock or a calendar page and give the French for it. Answers water the matching plots.
Question maker: turn a statement into a question in three ways, with est-ce que, by inversion or by tone. Each right form adds to your practice score.
Negation builder: fill in the pieces of ne pas, ne jamais and ne rien around a verb. Correct builds water the grammar plots.
Pronoun puzzle: place a pronoun such as lui, y or en in the right spot in a sentence. Each correct placement adds to the practice score and waters its plots.
Past tense chooser: read a short story cue and choose between the perfect and the imperfect, with a one-line reason shown after. Right answers water the tense plots.
Everyday documents: read a code-drawn menu, train timetable, shop sign or ticket and answer questions about it. Each right answer waters the plots for the words it used.
Cognate bridge: learn predictable endings that turn English words into French ones, such as ty to te, then guess new words. Right guesses water their plots.
Reading corner: short invented passages such as a postcard or an email, with true, false or not mentioned questions. Right answers water the plots behind the key words.
Verb spotlight: one verb at a time gets a full sheet with every tense and example sentences, then a quick quiz. Quiz answers water the verb's plots.
Silent letters: pick which letters in a word are not pronounced. Right picks add to the practice score and water the plot.

Case of the missing key: a mystery where the clues and alibis are short French sentences and you work out who did it. Reading each clue correctly waters the plots for its words, and solving the case adds a big practice bonus.
Treasure map: follow French directions such as turn left or go straight to move across a grid and reach the treasure. Each correct step waters the direction plots.

sections.title: Le Champ de Mots: made for you

items.text: Three standing goals: the farm shows three goals at all times in any order, such as "week 6 plots to Blooming", "200 practice points" and "10 plots Automated". You get the goal layout you like.
Greenhouse: each Automated plot becomes a small low-poly potted plant on a shelf in a dark greenhouse you can browse. You get a collection that shows how much you have learned.

Visiting student: a helper mode where you teach a small character by choosing which hint to give, and reviewing your own mastered plots is how you do it. You get a helper role that still counts as practice.
Moonlit style: another look for the farm with a dark sky, soft lamps and fireflies. You get a calm night setting that fits late-night study.
Bedtime ten: a fixed ten-question wind-down in the same order every night that ends by itself and shows your steady growth. You get a routine you know by heart.
Marathon plan: for long sessions, a four-stage checklist of warm-up, new words, weak words and a mini test, with a progress bar. You get shape for a three-hour stretch.

Pen-friend in Paris: a pen-friend texts you in simple French and you reply by choosing sentences, with branching paths; each correct reply waters the plots for its words. You get a Lifeline-style story that counts as practice (your Lifeline taste).
Silent watering-can robot: a small robot with expressive eyes reacts when plots grow or wilt. You get a quiet robot companion (your droid taste).

Verb compiler: assemble ending rules for each person to generate a verb's forms, and tests turn green as you get them right, each passing test watering the verb plots. You get a coding-style puzzle for French (your coding taste).

Word flow boards: connect French words to their English meanings with paths that cannot cross, Flow Free style; each pair waters its plot. You get a favourite puzzle that counts as practice (your Flow Free taste).

Grammar rule board: slide word tiles such as changing le to les to change a rule and open a gate; each correct change waters grammar plots. You get a Baba Is You style puzzle in French (your rule-puzzle taste).
Jars of beaten words: each stubborn word you finally master goes into a jar on a shelf. You get a collection of your hardest wins (your collect-everything taste).

Two-person translation: one friend sees the French, the other the English, and they talk it out in any app; each correct answer waters the plot for both. You get a co-op practice (your Keep Talking taste).
Cheer cards: leave a friend a preset French cheer such as Bravo on their farm. You get a friend tie with no chat (your gifts-and-notes taste).

Welcome-back rescue: after a break plots show as resting, and a ten-question rescue walk revives them together. You get a friendly return with nothing lost (your welcome-back and no-lost-progress taste).
Memory fog: plots you have not watered recently sit under soft fog that lifts when you water them. You get a moody picture of how fresh your memory is (your fog taste).
Hydroponic bay style: a visual style of a dark space-station garden with robots tending plants. You get a space look for the farm (your space and robots taste).
The crow: an optional dry, dark crow who comments in French and English, never about mental health. You get humour in your tone (your dry-and-dark taste).

French skill tree: a big tree of grammar and vocabulary skills where each node levels up as its plots grow, with no refunds. You get a big tree that counts as practice (your huge-skill-tree and Duolingo taste).
Smart-route badge: the farm notices when one answer waters several plots and logs the efficient routine you found. You get credit for a clever routine (your broken-build taste).
Words-seen counter: a lifetime counter of words seen that climbs into the thousands. You get numbers that grow big (your big-number taste).
Everyday rights pack: vocabulary for asking for help with health, housing and water, and for helping others. You get words for the things you care about (your human-rights taste).
Path stones: each three-minute quest lays a stone on the road to your exam. You get short wins that build a path (your short-wins taste).
Ask for a suggestion: a button that says "Would you like a suggestion?" and only then proposes the next activity. You get help only when you want it (your suggestion-only-if-asked taste).
Handed rule cards: each grammar topic hands you a one-card rule as it unlocks. You get handed rules (your handed-recipes taste).
Unpack the crate: label the items of a French household as you unpack them into a room, and each correct label waters its plot. You get a calm Unpacking-style game that counts (your Unpacking taste).
Calm farm: a mode with no goals, no golden plot and no combos shown, just plots. You get a quiet way to practise (your calm-mode taste).
Course completion bar: one percentage bar for plots Automated, games tried and tests passed. You get a reachable 100 percent (your reachable-100% taste).
Half-listening review: slow single-tap multiple choice with no combos, for class or when half asleep. You get review that needs little attention (your half-attention taste).
Banter pack: playful phrases to use with friends, kept friendly. You get French for the banter you love (your Among Us banter taste).

sections.title: Le Champ de Mots: PC view

items.text: Make Enter submit, Tab move to the next plot and the arrow keys walk the farm, with a keyboard-focus ring on the current plot. You can water the whole farm without the mouse.
Add an accent key layer where holding Alt and a letter types the French accented form (Alt+e gives é), with a small cheat chart in the corner. You type French fast on any PC keyboard.
Show a hover card on each plot with the word, its stage, next review date and last three answers. You see a plot's history by pointing.
Add a right-click menu on a plot with Water now, Add a note, Flag a mistake and Show cultural note. Study tools sit at the cursor.
Let you drag the Exam Planner, Phrasebook and Progress dashboard into a three-column study desk that remembers its size. A big monitor becomes a proper study station.
Add a keymap overlay on Shift+F1 that shows where é, è, ç and œ sit on US, UK and AZERTY layouts, with a click to type one. You type French accents without hunting.
Add Ctrl+K as a command palette that jumps to any word in your phrasebook, minigame or week by typing. You find a word in a few letters.
Add a Ctrl+F word search window that filters the farm by word, tag or stage and highlights matches. You find a word without scrolling.
Add a split phrasebook view with the word list on the left and the selected word's full detail on the right, with arrow keys to browse. You read vocabulary like a dictionary app.
Add a pinned side clock showing words due today and a progress ring on wide screens. Your study target stays in view.

sections.title: Le Champ de Mots: mobile view

items.text: Make watering a full-screen question card with a big on-screen accent bar and large answer buttons at the bottom. A study round is a one-thumb card.
Let a swipe from a plot to the right water it. The farm works by gesture.
Lift the question card and accent bar above the on-screen keyboard and add a Done key that closes it. Typing French on a phone never hides the question.
Add a bottom tab bar (Farm, Study, Games, Me) that stays on every screen. Moving round the app is one thumb tap.
Add a home-screen card with words due today, words known and your exam countdown before the farm loads. You can check study status in class.
Make a Five-minute set a single button that picks the right number of due words and ends with a summary card. A short session fits a break.
Add a portrait minigame lobby of large cards, one per minigame, with your best score on each. Practice games feel like a phone arcade.
Add an offline set of the next week's words that you can study fully without a connection. Study works on the bus.
Add a night-study mode that dims the farm, enlarges the cards and shows one question at a time. It suits bed-time play.
Add a landscape typing layout where the question sits above and the keyboard area shrinks to fit. Typing on a phone is less cramped.

sections.title: Le Champ de Mots: minigame ideas by week

items.text: Week 1, Clock Tower: read a clock face and tap the French time (minutes, quarter, half, "moins"), with each right answer adding a bell to the tower on your farm and counting toward the practice score.
Week 1, Timetable Dash: slide event cards onto the right hour of a day planner using 24-hour French times; every placed card counts as a watering.

Week 2, Morning Routine Builder: drag the reflexive verbs of a morning routine (se lever, se laver, s'habiller) into order and conjugate each for a given person; a finished routine becomes a small scene on your farm.
Week 2, Never Ever: a catch-the-sentence game where you place "ne ... jamais" around the verb in a moving line of sentences.
Week 3, Gym Bag: pack a bag for a leisure plan by matching items and activities to the French words; every packed item adds to your vocabulary count.
Week 3, Weekend Plans Match: pair people with the leisure activity they describe in a short French message.
Week 4, Ask Me Anything: turn answers into questions with the right question word, including the question word at the end of a sentence; each question counts as a watering.
Week 4, Calendar Day One: pick the right date for the first of the month ("le premier") among tricky date phrases in a stack of event cards.
Week 5, Fashion Show: dress a figure from a French description (colour and clothing words) and score by how many details you match.
Week 5, Colour Agreement: choose the right form of a colour or adjective for the noun it describes, in a quick card sweep.
Week 6, Boutique Opinions: give an opinion about an item in a shop window using the right shop and opinion phrase.
Week 6, Word Order Builder: rebuild a scrambled French sentence by dragging words into the correct order.
Week 7, Weather Wardrobe: look at a weather card and pick what to wear and pack, using the season phrases ("au printemps", "en été").
Week 7, Seven-Day Forecast: read a forecast and answer questions about each day, from the supplement's style of table.
Week 8, Market Stall: sort 50 food words into shelves and then buy a basket using the partitive and its exceptions (du, de la, des, "pas de").
Week 8, Likes and Dislikes Dinner: seat guests by what they like to eat and drink, using the liking verbs.
Week 9, Shopping List Run: fill a shopping list with the right quantities and fillings ("un kilo de", "à + article") across different shops.
Week 9, Replace It: swap a noun for "le, la, les" or "en" in a sentence, including with the futur proche.
Week 10, Passé Composé Postcards: write what happened by choosing the right helper verb and participle, with agreement of the object pronoun.
Week 10, Restaurant Order: take an order in French at a restaurant and answer the waiter with the right pronouns.
Cross-week, Story Chain: each round adds one sentence to a growing French story, and each sentence uses grammar from a different week, so the story becomes a record of everything you have practised.
Cross-week, Spot the Odd One: pick the word that does not belong from a mix of topics across several weeks, to tell similar topics apart.
Cross-week, Memory Pairs: match French words with English meanings or pictures from a chosen range of weeks.
Cross-week, Speed Sort: sort a deck of words into their weeks' topics, showing which topics are your weakest.
Cross-week, Day in Paris: a short guided day (wake up, shop, eat, talk about the weather and plans) that pulls questions from the weeks you pick, with a postcard at the end.
Cross-week, Verb Gym: conjugate verbs from several weeks in a short circuit, with a set count of reps and no timer.
Cross-week, Mistake Detective: find and fix the single error in a French sentence (agreement, word order, wrong helper verb) from any week.
Cross-week, Exam Warm-Up: a short mixed set shaped like the online written exam, built from the weeks covered so far, with a score you can compare over time.
Cross-week, Gender Garden: sort nouns from all weeks into le and la beds as they grow, tracking your gender accuracy.
Cross-week, Tutorial Remix: replay the question formats your own tutorials use (fill in the blank, matching, sentence rewrite) over words from the weeks you choose.
Cross-week, Pronoun Pinball: send each sentence's noun to the right pronoun slot (le, la, les, lui, en, y) as the ball bounces, calm and untimed.
Cross-week, Semester Map: a drawn map of the whole semester where each week is a town and each minigame played there lights it up, so you can see where you have practised least.
Blocked tiles: some tiles are rock, so you cannot ping there and signals are weaker across them. You get a new kind of puzzle with a map to read.
Mixed strengths: transmitters come in strong and weak types, and you mark which is which as well as where. You get a harder deduction for players who want more.
Fuzzy readings: in a special mode every reading can be off by one, and the board says so. You get a puzzle about reasoning with uncertain information.
Ping replay: after a solve, step back through your pings and watch the possible positions shrink. You get to see how a good solve works.
Curated packs: hand-made boards in named packs, such as Twins, Corner Cases and Hidden Pair. You get puzzles with a clever idea behind each one.
Make your own puzzle: place transmitters yourself, test that it can be solved, and get a code to share. You get to design puzzles for friends.
Technique lessons: short hand-built boards that each teach one trick, such as using a corner or comparing two readings. You get a gentle route from beginner to expert.
Wasted-ping review: after a solve, the game marks which pings gave no new information. You get a clear way to get closer to par.
Odd-shaped boards: rings, diamonds and L shapes in addition to squares. You get new puzzle looks with the same rules.
Drifting transmitter: one transmitter moves one tile after every ping in a pattern shown in advance. You get a puzzle about time as well as place.
Skill drills: practice sets focused on one situation, such as corner transmitters, two close together, or only on the edge. You get targeted practice for your weak spots.
Reading predictor: a quick drill where you are shown transmitters and guess what a ping at a tile would read. You get a sharper feel for the rule.
Month badges: complete every daily puzzle in a calendar month from the archive to earn a badge for that month. You get a calm collector's goal with no deadline.
Wide ping: a second tool that reads the total of a 3x3 area, costing more of your budget. You get a new strategic choice about how to spend pings.
Free listening: a practice mode with unlimited pings and no score. You get a relaxed place to explore and learn.
Pattern album: every layout of transmitters you meet, such as pairs, triangles and lines, is filed in an album with a count of how many you have discovered. You get a collector's page.
Quiet streak: the total number of puzzles you have solved is shown big and can never go down, with the streak small beside it. You get steady progress that cannot be lost.
Three goals panel: three standing goals, such as "ten Hard solves at par", "fill six album pages" and "three archive weeks". You get the goal layout you like.
Distress calls: each solve locates a lost probe on a sector map, and clearing a sector opens the next. You get short wins that build into a bigger picture, in space.

Two listeners: an invite link splits a board's pings between two players who each see only their own readings and talk it out in any app they like. You get an optional friend tie with no chat built in.

Night shift radio: a stranger's weak signal appears and you advise them over branching nights, as a hobbyist with a radio. You get a Lifeline-style story in the radio room (your Lifeline and radio-tinkerer taste).
Console AI: an optional console voice with dry, dark remarks about your pings, never about mental health. You get a GLaDOS-like character (your Portal taste).
Antenna mite: a tiny silent robot on the dish that shows emotion with its lights. You get a quiet robot companion (your droid taste).
Receiver parts: each achievement unlocks a radio part, such as an antenna or filter, displayed on a rack with a percentage bar. You get a one-of-each collection (your collect-everything taste).
Equation pad: write sum equations from your readings and the game checks that your logic holds without revealing answers. You get a maths tool for solving (your logic and maths taste).
Show the equations: after a solve, see the system of equations your pings made. You get a clear view of the maths (your maths taste).
Friends' album compare: see which pattern pages your friends have, counts only and no scores. You get a friend tie where nobody is worst (your hide-my-score taste).
Second listen: after a wrong answer you may trade your par medal for one more attempt. You get a restore instead of a fail (your restore-progress taste).
Low-poly observatory: a dark low-poly dish on a hill behind the board, lighting up as you ping. You get a moody scene (your dark low-poly taste).
Anomaly file: odd readings that break normal rules are named and catalogued, such as echo, ghost and drift. You get a creepy but calm collection (your anomaly-game taste).
Routine sweep: the same easy three-board warm-up in the same order, ending with a known sign-off. You get a routine you know by heart (your routine taste).
Slow tune set: very easy boards with big tiles for half-asleep play. You get puzzles that need no effort (your half-asleep taste).
The ladder: sixty boards from very easy to hard in small steps, with a clear 100 percent. You get an easy-to-start, built-up path (your built-up-difficulty taste).
Mastery bar: one percentage bar covering the album, ladder and archive. You get a reachable 100 percent (your reachable-100% taste).
Welcome-back line: the radio says it has been quiet and lists what changed in the archive. You get a friendly return (your welcome-back taste).
Wave lab: a playground with sliders showing how a signal fades with distance. You get a physics toy (your physics taste).
Glow level: a slider for the screen glow and scanline strength, with an off position. You get effects you control (your toggleable-effects taste).
Coverage map: a map of every tile you have ever pinged, with a percentage. You get exploration and completion (your exploration taste).
Vector theme: a green line-drawing look like an old vector display. You get a computer look (your Tron and computers taste).
Expert solve viewer: watch a strong solve at your own pace with the reasons beside each ping. You get the walkthrough built in (your watch-a-100%-run taste).
Puzzle notebook: a notebook page per puzzle for your notes that fills as you play. You get a notebook you are filling out (your notebook-collection taste).
Sonar skin: the same rules in a dark deep sea where transmitters are strange creatures named in a bestiary. You get a creepy ocean version (your dark-ocean taste).
Friend playlist: a friend picks seven boards for you to play at your own pace. You get a friend gift with no chat (your gifts-and-notes taste).
Receiver workshop tree: a big tree of practice-mode tools such as filters and extra ping types, with no refunds. You get a big tree (your huge-skill-tree taste).
Learn by pinging: the first board teaches every rule by doing, with no text. You get an intuitive start (your no-tutorial taste).
Show a faint preview on hover that lists what a ping on that tile would read for each possible transmitter distance. You pick your pings with more thought and fewer wasted ones.
Let a right-click on a tile toggle a small pencil "maybe" note in the corner that does not count as an answer. You can think on the board the way you do on paper.
Add a readings sheet beside the board that lists each ping's tile and number in sortable rows, with a click that highlights the tile. Your evidence sits in one table.
Add Ctrl+Z and Ctrl+Y for markers and pencil notes, with a visible history list. You can try theories and step back.
Hold Space to overlay each ping's reach rings across the whole board, so the overlap points show where a transmitter must sit. You can see the logic of the puzzle at a glance.
Show the archive as a wide month grid with hover previews of each puzzle's board size and your result. You browse past puzzles like a calendar app.
Add mouse-wheel zoom and drag pan for large practice boards, with a recentre key. Big boards stay comfortable on a monitor.
Hold Shift to draw a ruler line from the cursor tile to the nearest ping showing distance and reading difference. You check the geometry quickly.
Let a held mouse button sweep across tiles to mark or unmark them in one stroke. Filling in candidate tiles is fast.
Add a stats window that stays open beside the board with streak and par history as small charts. Your record sits in view while you solve.
Hold a tile to show a magnifier bubble above your finger with the tile's coordinate and a ping preview, so your thumb never hides the target. Precise tapping works on a small screen.
Put the Ping and Mark tool switch as two big buttons at the bottom edge. The main choice sits under your thumb.
Let a tap ping the tile and a long-press mark it, as an option in Settings. One finger does both jobs without a tool switch.
Add a haptic pulse on each ping that grows stronger with a bigger reading, where the browser allows. You feel how close you are.
Reopen on the exact half-solved board with pings and markers in place. A two-minute visit keeps all your reasoning.
Add a Today shortcut that opens straight into the day's puzzle from the home-screen icon. You get a one-tap start.
Let you swipe between Today, Archive and Practice as three full-screen tabs. Moving between modes is a flick.
Add a pure-black dark theme for OLED phones with brighter tile outlines. Bed-time play is easy on the eyes and the battery.
Open a small radial menu with Ping, Mark and Clear next to your finger when you long-press the board. You never travel to a toolbar.
Add pinch to zoom on large boards, with a double-tap to reset. Large practice puzzles remain tappable.
Planet 4, the word-order language: who did what to whom is shown only by the order of the signs, and the scenes make you work it out. You get a new kind of deduction after the sign-meaning languages.
Planet 5, the two-channel language: each sign carries a shape and a rhythm, and the two carry different parts of the meaning. You get the hardest and most surprising language in the set.
Trade tongue: a message that mixes words from two earlier planets, as people really do when they meet. You get a puzzle that rewards everything you already learned.
Eavesdrop scenes: you watch two aliens talk with no input from you, then work out what they said from how the world changes. You get a quiet new kind of scene that needs only watching.
Damaged message: a transmission arrives with one corrupted mark, and you work out which one from what the message must say. You get a small error-finding puzzle.

Species field notes: each planet's species has a short invented note about how they sense and live, which hints at why their language works the way it does. You get world-building that actually helps.
Side-by-side signs: pick any two signs from any planets and see them next to each other with where you saw them. You get an easy way to compare and spot patterns.
Scene lab: set up the world however you like, then see how the aliens would respond to any message you write. You get a free sandbox for testing your theories.
Scene scrubber: step through a scene frame by frame instead of only watching it play. You get time to study details that go by fast.
Short-speech medals: reach each contact goal with as few messages as possible and earn a medal for it. You get a replay challenge for players who have finished.
Drawn-in signs: signs appear as if drawn stroke by stroke, with an off switch for reduced motion. You get a nicer look for the central thing in the game.

Message drawer: after each planet, a stack of extra incoming messages that mix known words in new ways, each one decoded adding to a counter. You get plenty of practice and a number that visibly grows.
Two dialects: one planet has two speakers who use slightly different forms of the same language, and you find the differences. You get a puzzle about variation.
Planet completion bar: each planet shows how many of its signs you have confirmed out of the total, with no hint of which are wrong. You get a clear sense of progress that does not give answers away.
Number systems chart: after contact, a chart compares how each planet writes numbers. You get a satisfying overview of what you have decoded.
Grammar sketch: after contact, a one-page plain description of each language's rules, with a small diagram. You get a clear summary of what you learned.
Scene gallery: replay any scene you have seen from a gallery, in order, with your own notes beside it. You get an easy way to check your theory against the evidence.
Pattern highlighter: an optional ship tool that underlines marks that repeat across scenes without saying what they mean. You get help spotting patterns without being given answers.
Epilogue letters: after the ending, each species sends a short letter that reflects how you spoke to them, such as brief, chatty or polite. You get an ending that reacts to your style.
Sequence riddles: short bonus puzzles where a row of messages has a gap and you fill in the one that fits. You get extra puzzles in each language after the main route.
The machine planet: a language that is secretly a tiny machine instruction set, where you learn what each code does and then write a short program. You get computers and robots as the puzzle.

The broken guardian: a lone damaged robot on an abandoned station whose log you piece together, with a quiet, tragic story and optional reading. You get a character in the spirit of the ones you like.
Crew choices: between planets, short branching talks with the crew, with a captain who makes real mistakes and no effect on the puzzles. You get optional story told your way.
Glyph museum: all signs from every planet on one wall, with the meanings you have confirmed filling in. You get a collector's page.
Three open goals: three contact goals visible across planets at all times, in any order. You get the goal layout you like.
Listening post: a calm screen where the ship plays back messages you have already decoded as a quiet running log. You get a watch mode for late at night.
Branching voyage: choose which planet to visit next, and the crew react differently depending on your order. You get a Lifeline-style path with your own choices (your branching-story taste).
The silent courier: a drone that never speaks and answers only in the signs you have learned, its meaning growing as you learn. You get a quiet robot character who shows feeling (your droid taste).
Dry crew asides: dry, dark one-line asides added to the crew log, never about mental health. You get humour in your tone (your dry-and-dark taste).
Specimen shelf: objects seen in the scenes, such as lamps and trays, kept as specimens on a shelf. You get a one-of-each collection (your collect-everything taste).
Translator pair: one friend sees the scene, the other holds the notebook, and they talk it out in any app. You get a co-op puzzle (your Keep Talking taste).
Mystery message: make a short message from your languages for a friend to decode. You get a friend gift with no chat (your gifts-and-notes taste).
Grammar filter: decide which garbled messages obey a language's rules, like regular expressions. You get a coding-style puzzle (your coding taste).
Number bench: convert and add Pulse numbers with binary switches. You get a binary puzzle (your maths and binary taste).
Spectrum planet: a planet that speaks in light lines, and you decide which element each means. You get sci-fi science to decode (your chemistry and science-fiction taste).
Base puzzle: numbers written in base 5 or base 12 from tally marks. You get a maths puzzle (your maths taste).
Sign tiles: slide signs on a board to change a world rule in a small sandbox. You get a Baba Is You style puzzle (your rule-puzzle taste).
Path panels: draw a path through signs that spells a valid message. You get a Witness-style puzzle from the grammar (your Witness taste).
Evidence board: pin fragments of an impossible message and name what is sending it, creepy but calm. You get an investigation (your Phasmophobia-style taste).
Low-poly globes: each planet as a dark low-poly globe with its lamps lit. You get a moody look (your dark low-poly taste).
Previously on Marigold: a two-line recap of your last scene when you return. You get a friendly welcome back (your welcome-back taste).
Full completion bar: one percentage bar across signs, scenes and achievements. You get a reachable 100 percent (your reachable-100% taste).
Postcard mural: each decoded phrase sends a postcard home, and the postcards form a growing mural. You get short wins building a bigger picture (your short-wins taste).
Unpack the crate: place alien objects in a lab by following words. You get a calm Unpacking-like game (your Unpacking taste).
Linguist tree: a big tree of notebook tools unlocked by contact points, none of which gives answers away. You get a big tree (your huge-skill-tree taste).
Star map: faint signals on a star map that you tune to reveal their place and strength. You get exploration and completion (your exploration taste).
Riddle achievements: achievements with cryptic riddle descriptions. You get hidden goals that give a clue (your cryptic-description taste).
Confirm stamps: a tiny stamp animation each time a sign is confirmed. You get a small reward every few minutes (your small-rewards taste).
Sketch page: rough pencil sketches of each species in the crew notebook, drawn by code. You get a hand-drawn touch (your hand-drawn-on-occasion taste).

Contact settings: Gentle, Standard and Sharp settings that change the number of scenes and distractor signs, each checked to stay deducible. You get a difficulty you choose (your choose-difficulty taste).
Hover any sign to light up every place it appears in the scenes, notebook and crew log at once. You can spot patterns by pointing.
Show scene player, notebook and transmit bar as three docked panes with draggable dividers on wide screens. You can watch, note and compose together.
Let you drag signs from the notebook into the transmit bar and reorder them by dragging. Building a message feels hands-on.
Press / to search the notebook by sign shape or your own note, and arrow keys to move through the matches. You find an entry with the keyboard only.
Add a right-click menu on a sign with Add note, Show scenes and Copy to transmit. Common jobs sit at the cursor.
Pin a scene as a small floating player that stays visible while you edit the notebook. You can compare as you write.
Double-click a sign in a scene to jump the notebook to its entry and open it for editing. You go from scene to note in one action.
Add Ctrl+Z and Ctrl+Y for the transmit line. You can try a message and step back.
Show a hover line on each crew-log entry saying which planet and scene triggered it. You can trace the story to its cause.
Add a print layout so Ctrl+P produces a one-page glossary of your notebook. You get a take-away sheet of what you have decoded.
Play scenes as full-screen vertical cards where you swipe up for the next scene and tap to pause. Watching feels like a phone story.
Pull the notebook up as a bottom sheet with a peek height that leaves the scene visible above. You can read and watch together.
Make the transmit pad two big buttons for tick and bar, with a short buzz for a tick and a long buzz for a bar, where the browser allows. Composing a signal feels physical.
Add a portrait sign keyboard at the bottom with your known signs in a grid, tapped to build a message. Composing is a thumb job.
Let you long-press a sign in a scene to copy it into the transmit line. A sign moves from watching to speaking in one gesture.
Resume a scene at the exact frame you paused on. A short visit never loses your place.
Add a home-screen card with planets contacted, signs decoded and the next goal. You can see progress at a glance.
Add a dim night theme with softer glow on the signs. Bed-time puzzling stays gentle.
Turn the crew log into a swipeable card stack, one entry per card. Story beats fit a phone.
In landscape, show the scene on the left and the notebook on the right. Turning the phone gives a work desk.
A "walk-through" button on the plan screen that highlights which beats are crowded and which have slack, without running the heist. You see where a plan is thin before you commit.
Named plan slots for each target, so you can keep a safe plan and an ambitious plan side by side. You can switch between them in one tap.
A floor-plan sketch of each target that lights up the rooms the crew visit beat by beat. You can picture where things go wrong.
A tiny three-beat practice job at the pub that teaches placing, standby and pair clashes with no payout pressure. New players learn by doing before the first real target.
A "why is this risky?" line under each odds word (Solid, Risky, Long shot) naming the skill gap or trait behind it. Planning becomes readable instead of guessy.
A crew relationship web screen showing every friend and feud pair as a simple line map. You can see at a glance who to seat together or apart.
A complication codex that lists each complication you have met, how it started and what counters it. You build a reference you can plan from.
A sixth target, the Sleepy Opera House, with a long interval beat where a whole audience changes the crowd tags. You get a new puzzle shape, not just a new skin.
A "quick job" variant of each target with only four beats and fewer crew slots. You get a satisfying heist in a few minutes.
A plain-list playback view that reads each beat as short sentences with no animation. Screen-reader users and anyone on a slow phone get the full story.
A phone "one lane at a time" plan view that shows a single crew member's row full width with arrows to the next. Placing actions stays comfortable at 375px.
Tiny mood icons on crew cards (calm, jumpy, grumpy) that reflect their current friends and feuds. You read the room before the job starts.
A "cleanest job" record per target, showing the fewest complications you have ever had. You get a clear personal goal to replay for.
Alternate objectives per target (swap it, borrow it, leave something behind) that change the beat names and what counts as a win. Each target gets a second life.
After a botched job, a "what would have helped" note naming one change that would have absorbed the first link. Failure teaches instead of just stinging.
Crew biography cards that unlock one line per job worked together, building into a short portrait. You get to know people, not only skill pips.
Gear pairs, where two specific pieces carried together give a small bonus. You get a reason to experiment with loadouts.
A safehouse screen where loot buys cosmetic furniture, with a shelf of souvenirs from each target. The money turns into something you can look at.
A "show the chain" toggle during playback that draws arrows from each line back to the first link live, not only on the payout screen. Cause and effect is visible as it happens.
Larger-text and high-contrast presets on the plan grid, tested at 320px. The dense timeline stays usable for everyone.
A night version of each target with a different complication pool and a darker palette. Familiar jobs feel fresh without new levels.
A "copy plan as text" button that gives the timeline as plain rows. You can paste it into notes to compare ideas.
A bench view that lists crew you have not hired yet with the job where they first appeared. You know who you are missing.
A "swap two lanes" button that exchanges two crew members' whole rows. Trying a different seating takes one tap.
A "crew night in" scene between jobs where you pick two crew to share a table, nudging their friendship. Relationship building becomes a choice, not a side effect.
A Committee Codex that fills with every crew member, complication, gear piece and target seen, with a single percentage at the top. It feeds the collect-everything and reachable-100% taste.

Three always-visible goals strip at the top of the board, each a "get this to level 5" style target (a crew bond, a target mastery, a gear set). It gives you the three-goals-at-all-times layout you like.
A "Break the Job" achievement per target for finding the one wildly overpowered plan, logged in a Hall of Cheats page. It rewards the feeling of finding the broken build.
A "Suggest a plan" button that fills a safe plan you can edit. Late-night half-asleep planning stays easy.
A new target, the Moon Archive Vault, with low gravity beat names and robot guards. It brings space and robots into the caper.
A janitor robot crew member who talks in terse status lines and never makes small talk. It is a quiet character in the spirit of the tragic broken helpers you like.
A dark low-poly night-city theme for the plan screen and payout. It gives the moody look you prefer.
A Fixer mode where you plan jobs for a client crew of NPCs and are judged on how well you kept them safe and happy. It suits the helper-over-competitor role.
A "Who started it?" guess after each job where you pick the crew member behind the first link. It echoes the Among Us banter you enjoy.
A Rewind to any beat button during playback that restores the job to that moment to try a different plan. It is a restore point instead of failure.
A City Map that fills one district at a time as each short job is finished, so little wins form a bigger picture. It matches the short-wins-into-a-slow-arc taste.
A "Previously at the Committee" card on return that recaps the last job and one open goal. It gives the friendly welcome-back you asked for.
An auto-advance watch mode that plays a finished plan on a loop of replays at a gentle pace with a calm background. It is a leave-it-on-a-second-screen mode.
Puzzle Jobs with exactly one valid plan, such as seating five crew where each feud and friendship must be satisfied. It gives the spatial logic puzzle fix.
A graded hint ladder (nudge, hint, answer) on Puzzle Jobs. You never have to leave to look up a walkthrough.
Plan Rules, a small if-then panel where you write a standby rule like "if alarm, Dot holds the door". It brings coding-style logic into the plan.
A Strategy Notes page listing the known strong pairings per target, unlocked as you discover them. You never need to alt-tab for a build.
A branching choice before each Committee meeting (take the safe offer or the odd one), with consequences in the debrief only. It gives Lifeline-style choices without a visual novel.
A crew thread where one quiet ex-guard decides between three loyalties across many jobs, with a different banter line per choice. It scratches the branching-story itch while staying optional.
An opt-in Ironman badge that locks the plan after you press Start with no retry. It gives hard mode as an option, never the base game.
An "Optimiser" stats page showing your best payout per target and the plan that earned it. It serves the optimising play style.
A private invite-code board for friends showing only each person's cleanest-job count, with hide-my-score. It is an optional friend tie without chat.
A "lend a crew member" card that lets a friend borrow one of your unlocked crew for a single job. It creates a friend tie that needs no messages.
Every crew member gets one visible flaw that costs them, with no all-good hero in the roster. It follows your dislike of faultless heroes.
A one-handed plan mode with large tap targets and a Next-lane button. It suits playing from bed.
Dark-humour debrief lines that stay dry and deadpan, never silly or meme-based. It matches your humour.
A Hacker Terminal job told entirely through a terminal log, where each plan beat is a command you type from a short list. It blends computers with the caper.
A "Collection night" list of the three closest-to-complete things (crew, gear, complications) with the exact job that would finish each. It makes finishing easy.
A Glitch log that records every deliberate harmless exploit you find, such as two clashing crew absorbing each other. It feeds the build-breaking fan.
A session goal picker on the opening screen (finish one target, meet one new crew member, fill one codex page) that gets ticked at the end. It honours proud-of-a-self-set-goal sessions.
Show a hover card on each timeline cell with its odds in words, who clashes with whom there, and what chains it could set off. You plan with the facts in front of you.
Add a right-click menu on a cell with Clear, Copy to another beat, Swap with and Show odds. Cell jobs sit at the cursor.
Let a drag-box select several cells and arrow keys nudge the whole block one beat. You can shift a plan without redoing it.
Add Ctrl+C and Ctrl+V to copy a block of actions from one crew row to another. You reuse a good routine.
Add a playback film strip under the timeline with J, K and L stepping, a speed key and a draggable playhead. You can study exactly how a complication chained.
Highlight every cell changed since your last run with a small dot, and list them in a side panel. You can see what your edits did.
Add a second-screen playback log with big text you can pop out into its own window. The story plays on one screen while you plan on the other.
Add a pop-out client brief window you can park on a second monitor, listing the target's rules and complications. The brief stays visible and the timeline gets the full screen.
Add a Controls tab in Settings that rebinds the arm keys 1 to 9, Standby and Delete. The keys fit your hand.
Hover a crew portrait to show its clash and friendship pairs as small icons in the side panel. You can seat the crew without opening a screen.

Show the timeline one crew row at a time, with swipe up and down between crew and sideways scroll for beats, and a bottom sheet to pick an action for a tapped cell. Planning works on a portrait screen.
Put the action tray as a thumb-height carousel at the bottom with the odds shown as one word. You pick an action in one flick.
Add a short buzz for each link in a complication chain during playback, where the browser allows. A chain reaction is felt.
Play the heist as full-screen story cards where a tap anywhere moves to the next beat. Playback is a one-thumb show.
Resume playback at the exact beat you left. A two-minute pause never loses the story.
Let a long-press on a cell open a sheet that explains its odds in plain words. Detail comes without a hover.
Let the crew sheet slide in from the left edge with a swipe and slide away with another. The timeline gets the whole screen when you plan.
In landscape, show the whole timeline with crew rows and allow a pinch to zoom. Turning the phone gives the full plan view.
Add a dim cosy-night theme with bigger cells. Bed-time planning stays easy.
Add a swipe on a past job in the career list to replay it. History is one flick away.
A tide gauge on the rock scene that shows high and low water with a number and a pattern. Dock work and boat visits become something you can plan around.
A second light on a far rock that you can visit by rowboat on calm days and tend for a night. The sim gets a new place without a new rule set.
A night preview that sketches the next night's arrivals as small silhouettes on the horizon bar. You plan oil with more than the barometer.
A "lamp schedule" template saver, so you can name a plan like "Fog night" and reuse it. Evenings go faster once you know your routine.
A seasonal harvest on the island garden where each season grows different things that unlock different meals. The year has a visible shape.
A short morning "keeper's weather word" that names the sky in plain language (a mackerel sky, a flat calm). The morning report feels more like a place.
A "what happened last night" timeline that replays the night as a row of icons you can tap for details. You can understand a bad night after the fact.
Visiting inspectors who arrive by boat a few times a year and ask a friendly question about how you keep the station. Each visit gives a small reward for what you built.
Weather icons with a pattern for each type, tested at high contrast. Fog, squall and storm are never told apart by colour.
A calm-sea "stargazing" view on clear nights that draws the constellations that sit over your rock. Quiet nights have something to look at.
A tower-top telescope that lets you pick a passing ship to follow and read its small ship's record. Ships become characters, not dots.
A "repair preview" that shows what a repair will cost in supplies before you spend it. Day planning stops being a guess.
Larger-text and low-motion presets that keep the beam as a static cone with a tick mark. The scene is readable for everyone.
A winter sea-ice mode where ice forms on the dock and needs clearing, with its own set of upgrades. The seasons change what you do, not just numbers.
A "quiet hours" setting that shortens the evening plan to three taps with sensible defaults. Familiar nights go quickly.
A tidy-the-room mini ritual where you set out the sailors' gifts on shelves in any arrangement. The keeper's room becomes yours.
A fixed set of hand-made special nights, such as a meteor night or a still-air night, that each give a unique scene. Variety that is authored, not random.
A glossary tooltip for every lighthouse word (gallery, lens, cistern, lantern room) in plain language. New players learn the place as they play.
A "thank you" note that appears after a sailor's ship passes safely a third time. Repeat visitors feel noticed.
A harbour chart on the wall that fills with every route ships take past your rock. You see the traffic you made safe.
A year-in-review card at the end of each year with oil used, ships passed and nights quiet. The long play session gets a satisfying wrap.
Optional auto-wind for the clockwork once you own the right upgrade, with a visible indicator. Players who dislike a repeated chore can retire it.
A visiting painter who comes for a season and paints the rock in different weather, leaving pictures you can hang. The island gains art from your own nights.
A "mend order" button that sorts repairs by how worn each part is. Day plans take one tap when you do not want to think.
A "pause on event" switch that pauses whenever a ship arrives or weather turns. Slow thinkers can play without racing the beam.
A Keeper's Collection page with slots for every ship type, shell, feather and odd object found on the rock, each with a completion percentage. It feeds the collect-everything taste.
A "Nothing Happened" goal that counts quiet nights toward a visible bar. It rewards the calm-streak feeling without a lose condition.
Three standing goals pinned to the top of the day screen, each a "get this part to level 5" target (lens, cistern, dock). It gives the always-visible three-goals ideal.
A Watch Mode where the keeper runs the routine on a second screen at slow speed while you do something else. It suits leaving a game on while studying.
A "good-night" mode that dims the scene to a warm low-contrast palette, enlarges buttons and autopilots a standard night. It fits bed-time half-asleep play.
A welcome-back letter from the supply-boat captain that summarises where you stopped, every time you return. It delivers the friendly welcome-back.
A robot lighthouse-keeper's helper called Wick, a small wind-up machine that learns one chore at a time from you. It folds robots into the setting.
A moon-base lighthouse skin that swaps the sea for a lunar bay and the ships for landers. It gives the space theme as a switchable look.
A star-chart wall that fills with real constellations, each with its source named on screen. It mixes space with a notebook being filled in.
A tower-top computer terminal that logs readings and can be programmed with simple rules, such as "if fog, set Bright". It brings coding logic into the keep.
A Pattern Lock puzzle for the old workshop door, a small logic puzzle that opens a new shelf of tools. It gives a spatial puzzle fix inside the cozy sim.
A "restore the night" button on the morning report that replays the evening plan from the start. A bad night becomes a retry, not a loss.
A branching letter exchange with one sailor where your replies shape three possible endings of their story. It follows the Lifeline-style branching taste.
A friend lantern, where a friend who also plays can light a small lamp on your horizon once, without any message. It creates an optional friend tie.
A "shortest way to 100%" list showing exactly which three things are left, such as a gift or a mystery. It makes finishing easy.
A quiet ex-keeper character living in the fog bell house, who barely speaks and shows a worn past in his objects. He is a broken-but-gentle figure like the ones you like.
A dark, earthy night palette with a low-poly rock silhouette option. It matches your moody visual taste.
Sailor flaws, such as a boastful captain or a nervous cook, who each make one real mistake and apologise. It avoids all-good heroes.
A "break the system" achievement for finding a harmless wick trick that burns half the oil, logged in a Clever Things page. It honours the joy of finding the broken build.
A Mystery Notebook where each odd detail is a clue page that you fill in as you reason out its warm answer. It gives the investigative Phasmophobia feel with no fear.
A setting for "session goals" like "meet one new sailor" that the morning report ticks off. It supports self-set goals for short sessions.
A one-handed mode that moves every control into the bottom third of the screen. It fits playing from bed.
An optimiser's worksheet that charts oil used per lamp-hour and suggests an efficient routine. It serves the quiet optimising style.
A seasonal "quiet routine" card that saves your favourite plan and applies it with one tap. It matches a routine they know by heart.
A calm-sea screensaver mode that shows the beam turning with the date and nothing to click. It is a watch-and-relax moment.
A "steady progress" bar that only ever goes up across the year with no resets. It reflects progress that can never be lost.
A walkthrough ladder on every mystery with a nudge, a clue and the answer. You never have to leave the game to look it up.
A friendly rock gull that you can name and feed, with a small collection of its habits you discover. It is a gentle helper-role caretaker idea.
Optional dry, dark jokes in the keeper's logbook that stay gentle and never silly. It matches your humour.
A "short wins" shelf where each completed night leaves one small object (a pebble, a feather) on the windowsill. Small nights build into a full shelf.
Make the lighthouse picture clickable: hover the lamp, clockwork or trouble spot to see a glowing label and click to act. The keeper's rounds happen in the place itself.
Show a hover card on a ship with its name, cargo, mood toward the light and last letter. You read the sea by pointing.
Add a Controls tab in Settings that rebinds W, T, Space, brackets and the lamp keys. The keys fit your hand.
Make the letters window a two-pane mail reader with J and K to move between letters, the sailor on the left and the letter on the right. Reading is smooth.
Add a small storm scope as a dockable circular window you can place anywhere. You watch the weather without changing screens.
Add HUD scale and fade sliders in Settings, with an option to hide the HUD while nothing needs you. The scene stays cinematic.
Add a camera key C that cycles three fixed views (the sea, the gallery and the lantern room) with a slow drift. The place feels like a world you look around.
Save window arrangements such as "Keeper desk" and "Quiet night" and switch with F1 and F2. The screen fits the sitting.
Add a letterbox cinema option with a choice of 16:9 or 21:9 framing and optional film grain. The scene is framed like a short film.
Add an opacity slider for each window so reports and letters can sit as see-through panels over the scene. You read while the sea stays in view.
Make lamp level a tall slider at the right edge you drag with your thumb, with four marked notches. The main control is easy to reach.
Wind the clockwork by drawing circles on a crank on screen. A tap job becomes a small physical act.
Add an optional soft pulse once per beam sweep, off by default, where the browser allows. The light has a gentle rhythm you feel.
Show letters as paper cards you flip with a tap and swipe away to file. Reading feels like handling mail.
Keep a night summary strip in the header that expands into the full phase report when tapped. The main screen stays about the light.
Open the letters drawer with a swipe from the left edge. Reading mail is one thumb flick away.
Make the scene a tall portrait view with the lighthouse on top and phase panels in a bottom sheet. The place fits a phone.
Add a battery-saver night that draws one still frame and a moving beam only. The phone lasts through a long watch.
Keep four lamp-level buttons as a one-thumb rail on the bottom edge. Quick changes are one tap.
Show oil and repair as large icons with numbers in the top bar that glow gently when low, never loudly. Warnings are calm and clear.
A "recipe book" page that shows every merge chain you have made as a picture strip, tier by tier. New players learn what leads to what without guessing.
A hint highlight that circles the single best merge when you tap a "Help me" button, never costing a beat. Stuck players get unstuck without leaving.
A sixth goods family (candles and lamps) with its own five tiers and art. The board gets new combinations to chase.
A "preview the next crate" row so you can see what each crate will drop, one step ahead. Planning merges becomes a choice, not a gamble.
A seasonal cycle of themed festival backdrops (spring blossoms, autumn leaves) that change the stall art but not the rules. The market feels like it moves through a year.
A customer gallery that records every archetype with a one-line note on how to serve them best. Learning the cast becomes part of play.
Larger crates and grid cells as a display option, tested at 320px. Younger and older players can tap precisely.
A neighbouring stall you can visit between days, where a friendly trader swaps one of your spare goods for a decoration. Trading adds a gentle second loop.
A "slow lane" setting that doubles every customer's patience for players who prefer to think. The pledge stays intact because it counts beats, not time.
A "show what is possible" toggle that dims any good that cannot currently merge. Reading the board gets easier for beginners.
A weather layer for the stall (rain, sun, wind) that changes which customers show up and is previewed the day before. Days feel distinct without being random.
A summary chart at the end of each day showing orders served, tips earned and combos reached as plain bars with numbers. You can see how you improved.
A "colour-free goods" display that adds a shape and a letter to each family. The board works for every kind of colour vision.
A Stall Tour, a gallery view of your decorated stall from several angles with a photo mode that adds no text. Your decorations get shown off.
A tip jar history showing the generous things customers said. Tips feel like messages, not only numbers.
A "practice board" where you can freely place any goods to try chains, with no customers. You can rehearse a cascade at leisure.
A regulars' storyline arc extension with a fourth bond level for every regular that unlocks one more story scene. Long-time players keep finding new beats.
A reduce-motion setting that makes merges snap instead of slide. The board is calmer and easier on the eyes.
A cat that wanders the stall and sits on whichever decoration you last changed. A small reaction makes decorating feel alive.
A "Master Craft" order type that asks for a three-part chain of tier-5 goods, offered as an optional challenge with a unique decoration. Experts get a goal beyond the campaign.
A "last move" undo that takes back a single placement or merge without costing a beat. Fat-finger moves on a phone do not hurt.
A Free Stall mode setting that lets you pick the festival you want to play under. You can enjoy a favourite day again.
A market map showing the town around the stall, with each regular's home that appears after their third bond level. The community feels like a place.
A coin goal marker on the shop screen that shows how far off your next upgrade is. Saving up becomes easier to plan.
A "what changed since you played" note on return that lists new decorations or regulars unlocked. Returning players know where to look.
A Bazaar Catalogue where every good at every tier, every customer type and every decoration has a slot, with a percentage that is easy to push to 100. It feeds the collector and 100% taste.
Three goals always on the day screen, each phrased "bring this to level 5" (renown, a stall upgrade, a regular's bond). It gives the three-visible-goals ideal.
A "Whole market" overview page that shows all five families, six festivals and twelve regulars as a single progress map. It adds the bigger picture to each short day.
A Fixer's Corner where you help a regular fix a bigger problem in town by supplying goods over several days, no deadlines. It suits the helper-role taste.
A robot customer archetype who orders in precise numbers and tips in unusual coins, with a quiet voice. It brings robots and a quiet character into the market.
A Space Bazaar festival set where the stall moves to an orbital market with low-poly crates. It gives space and a dark low-poly look.
A dark, moody theme with a lantern-lit stall and an earthy palette. It matches the dark and earthy visual taste.
A Logic Crate puzzle mode, where a fixed board must be cleared with a set number of merges, one clean solution each. It scratches the spatial logic puzzle itch.
A graded hint ladder on Logic Crate puzzles (nudge, hint, answer). You never need a walkthrough.
A Watch Stall mode where the day plays itself at a slow pace using the best known moves while you look on. It suits leaving the game on a second screen.
A "good-night" mode with a dim warm palette, big touch targets and one-handed reach. It fits half-asleep play from bed.
A welcome-back line from the nearest regular that mentions your last combo. It gives a friendly return.
A "restore the day" button that replays any finished day from its start with the same orders. A bad day is never a loss.
A story-branch regular, the old tinker, whose three story paths depend on small choices about what to sell him. It is a branching story without a visual novel.
A "break the market" achievement for finding the best unintended coin trick, such as selling a wildcard at the right tier, recorded in a Clever Moves page. It rewards finding the broken build.
A self-set day goal picker (reach combo x3, serve ten, collect one decoration) shown at the day start and ticked at the end. It supports proud-of-your-own-goal sessions.
A coding-style Rule Board where you set simple priority rules like "serve haggler first" and watch them play a practice day. It brings a gentle coding puzzle into the stall.
A friend stall, where a friend's decoration set appears on a stand outside yours once, with no chat. It creates an optional friend tie.
A Collector's Fair with a rotating wall of rare decorations unlocked purely by the Catalogue percentage. It rewards completionists with something to look at.
An opt-in Ironman day where a missed order ends the day with no restore, badged as hard mode. Hard mode stays optional.
A short-wins board that stamps one small icon for each finished day, so ten days make a mural. It turns little sessions into a bigger picture.
A caretaker role where you restock a community pantry from spare goods and watch the town's shelves fill. It fits the helper taste with a food theme.
A strategy page of known best chains, unlocked as you find them. You can optimise without leaving.
A flawed regular, a vain collector who snubs the stall and later apologises. It avoids the all-good hero.
An optimiser view of coins earned per beat across your best days. It suits the optimiser style.
A dry, dark joke in each regular's third story line, nothing silly. It matches your humour.
A multi-viewpoint festival story told once from the stall owner, once from a customer, once from a rival. It follows your like of several points of view.
A steady-progress bar for the whole market that only moves up and never resets. It reflects progress that cannot be lost.
A rare-goods spotlight on the stall counter that shows the one item you are closest to collecting. It makes the last piece easy to find.
A "routine day" button that repeats your last day's choices so a familiar flow takes a few taps. It suits the routine-they-know-by-heart calm.
Hover a piece to highlight every piece it can merge with and show what the merge would make. You see good moves before you take them.
Add a right-click menu on a piece with Sell, Hand over to a customer and Pick up. Piece jobs sit at the cursor.
Hover a customer to show their liked goods and patience in beats. You can read the queue without opening anything.
On wide screens, let you drag decorations around a free-form stall scene to arrange them anywhere. Your stall becomes your own layout.
Hold Shift to select several pieces and press D to hand them all to one customer. A big order is one action.
Show a large chain counter on wide screens that grows and changes style as a combo builds. A good combo feels like a moment.
Add a board size slider from 80 percent to 160 percent in Settings. The board fits any monitor.
Hold Alt to show the hotkey number over every crate and tool. You learn the keys by looking.
Add a Controls tab in Settings that rebinds the crate, hand-over, sell and broom keys. The keys fit your hand.
Add save slots as a file-style list with coins, day and a small stall thumbnail. Loading looks like a real PC menu.
Let you flick a piece in a direction to push it to the next cell. Merging works by swiping.
Add a haptic tap on a merge that gets stronger with the tier and a roll for a cascade, where the browser allows. Merging feels satisfying.
Put Sell, Broom and Hand over as three big buttons along the bottom edge. The tools sit under your thumb.
Make the board fill the phone width with customers as a row of cards above it. The whole stall fits one portrait screen.
Let you pull down the stall banner to peek at the festival and regulars. A glance does not leave the board.
Resume the day on the exact board. A short break never loses a merge.
Show each customer's patience beats as large dots under their card. You never miss that someone is about to leave.
Let a double-tap on a piece pick it up and a double-tap on a customer hand it over. Frequent actions become gestures.
Add a mirror switch that moves the tool buttons to the left side. Left-handed play is comfortable.
Add a dark lantern-lit night market theme with larger pieces. Bed-time play stays easy on the eyes.
A "protractor overlay" on the chart that shows a bearing arc from your ship's start as you drag the heading. Setting headings feels like holding a real tool.
A short "what went wrong" ribbon on the reveal card naming the single leg that added most of the error. Players know exactly where to fix.
A seventh chapter of night passages where landmarks vanish and only a lighthouse flash pattern is visible at times. Planning needs a new kind of fix.
A "ghost your last attempt" overlay that draws your previous true track faintly under the new one. You can see if a change helped.
A chart notes box where you can type a few words that stay attached to that chart. Players can leave themselves reminders.
A harbour pilot mode where you steer into a tight harbour with a series of small legs and stationary fixes. It is a close-quarters challenge after open water.
A colour-free display of currents with distinct arrow styles for set and drift. The chart stays readable for every kind of colour vision.
A "pause the sail" scrub bar that lets you step through the true track in quarter-hour steps. You can study exactly where the sea pushed you.
A teaching chart set called Basics Bay with ten very short charts that each introduce one tool, such as leeway or tide. New players ramp up gently.
A tiny glossary for set, drift, leeway, fix and bearing, shown from any underlined word. Players learn terms while playing.
A tracked "closest to target" record per chart shown beside the stars. Every chart has a precise personal goal beyond the three stars.
A weather-front chart where the wind shifts partway through on a printed schedule in the chart's notes. Planning has to stage the passage.
A "compare to the par plan" view that lays the par route over yours with differences listed in plain words. You learn why the par works.
A reduce-motion option that shows the sail as a finished track with no animation. The reveal is calm and fast.
A harbour-side almanac that fills with the facts you use in play (set, drift, leeway rule), each with a named source on screen. It is a notebook that grows with you.
Larger steppers and quick-turn buttons with 44px targets at 320px. Setting legs on a phone gets easier.
A "snap to the flag" button that suggests a first heading toward the destination ignoring currents. Beginners get a start point.
A scenic chart pack of invented islands each with a short captain's note, solved in any order. Players can choose their favourite waters.
A list of your personal bests in the captain's log, one line per chart. Past results stay easy to find.
A mid-sail "alert" line when a hazard enters the ship's expected corridor in Watch-by-watch mode. The tool feels closer to a real watch officer.
A tide table builder where you draw the stream for a chart yourself from given high and low times. It teaches the idea by letting you build one.
A "steer by landmark" mode in open-water charts where you aim at a named point instead of a number. It gives a gentler way into the chart.
An optional ruler tool that measures distance and bearing between any two points you tap. Planning gets more precise.
A hand-drawn paper theme for the chart with textured edges and ink stains. It gives a very different look to the same charts.
A short post-chapter recap card listing the new tool you learned and one chart where you used it best. Each chapter closes with a clear step.
A Navigator's Collection with a slot for every chart's three stars, every hazard found, every landmark and every clever shortcut, with one percentage. It feeds the collect-and-100% taste.
Three goals always visible on the picker, each "get this chapter to 100 percent of stars" type. It gives the three-goals-at-all-times layout.
An orbital chart chapter where the sea becomes a gravity-field map and the ship becomes a probe, using the same plan-then-reveal flow. It brings space into the design.
A tidy low-poly map style that draws land as flat shaded polygons on a dark sea. It matches the dark and low-poly visual taste.
A "creepy ocean" wreck-field chart pack where the hazards are old hulls and the log lines stay gloomy but never harmful. It uses the ocean theme in the dark way you accept.
A programmable autopilot where you write a short list of rules, like "if drift over 2, steer 5 degrees up-current", then watch it sail. It adds a coding puzzle on top of navigation.
A "Script the leg" tester that checks your autopilot rules against every chart you have cleared. You get a logic puzzle with instant feedback.
A rescue chapter where you plot a safe path to bring a drifting vessel home, with no one harmed on screen. It fits the helper-over-competitor role.
A restore point button on the reveal card that jumps back to the legs you had before sailing. A bad attempt is a retry, not a loss.
A welcome-back line from the captain's log that names the chart you left unfinished. It gives a friendly return.
A Watch Mode where a finished par plan sails itself at slow speed on a loop of charts. It suits a second-screen calm.
A half-asleep mode with a big heading dial, three quick-turn buttons and dim colours. It fits bed-time one-handed play.
A Break the Chart achievement for finding a route that passes the rules in an unintended way, listed in a Clever Routes page. It rewards finding the broken build.
A branching logbook where a few chart choices decide the captain's route home across a long voyage. It gives Lifeline-style branching without a visual novel.
A quiet ship's AI character called Bellwether who gives terse notes and never boasts. It is a gentle machine voice in the spirit of the quiet characters you like.
A flawed navigator in the log who makes a clear mistake and owns it. It avoids the faultless hero.
A short-wins voyage map that stamps a port for every chart cleared, so small charts build into a long voyage. It suits the short-wins arc.
A walkthrough ladder on every chart with a nudge, a hint and the full par plan. You never have to leave to look it up.
A "Chart Notebook" mode where you sort cleared charts into your own folders and tag them. It suits note-taking collectors.
A friend ghost, where a friend's best track on a chart can be shown faintly under yours with no chat. It makes an optional friend tie.
An opt-in Ironman chart rule where grounding ends the run with no retry. Hard mode stays optional.
A session-goal picker (clear two charts, find one hazard, reach one star) ticked on the log at the end. It supports self-set goals.
A computer-lab chapter where you check the ship's navigation computer by working the maths by hand on the same chart. It blends computers with the sea.
A steady-progress bar for the whole campaign that only moves up and never resets. It reflects progress that cannot be lost.
A route-efficiency page ranking your tracks by error per hour. It suits the optimiser style.
A dry dark note in the captain's log after a grounding, such as "the rock won the argument". It matches your humour.
Multi-viewpoint voyages told by a captain, a pilot and a passenger, each seeing the same chart differently. It matches the like of several points of view.
A "closest to 100 percent" list that shows the three nearest completions and the exact chart for each. It makes finishing easy.
A one-tap "repeat my usual plan" button that loads the last plan you used for the same chart type. It suits a known routine.
A friendly welcome tile on first launch showing three kinds of play (chart solver, collector, scripter) and letting you pick one. It makes the game feel made for whoever opens it.
Let you type a leg as "090 6kn 2h" in a one-line box and press Enter to add it. Planning is fast for keyboard users.
Add mouse-wheel zoom and drag pan on the chart with a scale bar and a recentre key. You can read a big chart closely.
Show the position in nautical miles, the current arrow and the tide at that spot as you hover over the chart. The chart tells you what is under the cursor.
Add a right-click menu on the chart with Drop a fix mark, Measure from the ship and Add a waypoint. Chart tools sit at the cursor.
Hold R and drag to measure distance and bearing like parallel rules. You get a real chart tool.
Add a layers panel to toggle currents, wind, hazards, grid and labels. The chart can be as plain or rich as you like.
Add an editable plan table where every leg is a row with heading, speed and time cells you tab through, and the chart redraws as you type. You can plan like a spreadsheet.
Dock the tide table as a window beside the chart and highlight the row for the hour of your current leg. You read tides without hunting.
Add a Ctrl+P print layout that produces a clean chart sheet with your plan listed. You get a paper chart to keep.
Add save slots as a file-style list with chart name, stars and a thumbnail of the track. Loading looks like a real PC menu.
Set speed and time with two large wheel pickers at the bottom of the screen. Entering a leg is a thumb spin.
Let you pinch to zoom the chart and drag to pan. The chart works like a phone map.
Long-press the chart to drop a fix mark. A common job becomes a gesture.
Add a short buzz when the reveal shows your estimate within one nautical mile, where the browser allows. Accuracy is felt.
Show legs as cards you swipe to delete with an undo bar. Editing a plan is a flick.
Make the chart fill a portrait screen with the plan as a bottom sheet that peeks up. The chart and plan share a phone.
Resume the plan you were drafting, with every leg kept. Short visits never lose a plan.
Let the leg editor float as a draggable card over the chart that you can slide to the top or bottom. You keep the part of the chart you are working on in view.
In landscape, show the chart full-screen with a floating leg editor. Turning the phone gives a chart table.
Make downloaded charts work fully offline with a small list of what is saved. Navigation works on the bus.
A "Many tellings" panel on every contested event that shows how three different sourced viewpoints describe it side by side. You see that a disputed event can be told more than one way and why.
A Sources Library page for each set listing every source with how many claims it backs and who published it. You can see at a glance how well supported a set is.
An era lens filter on the archive (politics, economy, daily life, technology). You can look at one thread of the story without the rest.
A hand-drawn world map view where each event and person sits at its place. You see where history happened, not only when.
Timeline zoom levels (decade, century, whole set). You can place cards on a scale that suits the set.
A date-style setting for BCE/CE and other dating notes, with a plain explainer on how each works. Ancient sets read clearly instead of confusingly.
Word-help popups on unusual terms in the readings, each one sourced. You never have to leave the game to look up a word.
A short or full reading toggle for every passage. You choose how much to read for each session.
A person page for each figure collecting every claim about them, including the sources that disagree. You get a balanced portrait, not a hero or villain.
A "Copy my study sheet" button that turns what you have unlocked in a set into plain text with its sources. You keep notes you can use outside the game.
A compare mode that lays two sets on parallel strips, such as Greece beside the history of food. You spot what was happening in both at the same time.
A place-matching puzzle where you drop events onto the right spot of the map. You learn geography through events.
An "order by size" puzzle for quantities such as populations or distances, with each figure read live from a named source. You build a feel for scale.
Primary-source quote cards, each with a plain-language gloss beside it. You read real voices without getting lost in old wording.
A "load your own set" option that checks a JSON file with the same rules (three sources, dates, no contradictions) before it plays. You can make or try a set on any topic.
Difficulty presets for timeline puzzles (fewer cards, more hints, wider windows). You choose how hard each puzzle is before you start.
A hint ladder that first points at the era, then narrows the range, then names the neighbouring card. You get unstuck without being given the answer.
A one-line "why this order" note after each solved timeline that names the cause linking two cards. You learn the reason, not just the position.
A small lesson on primary, secondary and later sources with one worked example from the set. You understand the labels the game uses.
A Misconception Cabinet shelf in each set that holds every myth you have sorted, with what the record shows. You collect the popular stories that turned out wrong.
Life-span bars for each person drawn across the timeline. You see who overlapped with whom.
A "who really said it" mini-puzzle that sorts famous quotes into documented, disputed or doubtful. You learn which sayings to trust.
A network view showing how people, places and events connect as a web you can tap through. You find links you would not meet in a straight timeline.
Private notes you can attach to any claim, kept on your device. You keep your own questions next to the facts.
A coverage strip per set showing which eras are well sourced and which are thin. You see honestly where the game's knowledge is weak.
A three-goals strip always on screen, such as "find 3 more people", "clear one web chapter", "sort 5 myths". You always know the next three steps without a fixed order. (taste: three visible goals)

A 100% checklist page per set listing exactly which people, places, events and claims are still missing and which mode finds each. Nothing is hidden, so completing a set is reachable. (taste: collecting and 100%)
A quiet archivist character whom you help repair damaged records by putting scraps back in place. You play a helper whose work visibly restores a shelf. (taste: helper roles)
A dark low-poly vault drawn in code, with shelves, lamps and cases where each found item sits. You walk through a moody archive that fills as you learn. (taste: dark low-poly looks)
